1-5.translation:
Just as on a dark night, within the womb of clouds,
A flash of lightning shows brilliant illumination for an instant,
Likewise, by the power of the Buddha, occasionally
Intelligence for merit arises for a moment in the world.

issues.span: within the womb of clouds
issues.evidence: Tibetan སྤྲིན་རུམ་ན (Skt meghaghanāndhakāre) means 'in the thick mass of clouds'; bo-kunpal 1-5 glosses it as སྤྲིན་རུམ་ 'cloud-bank'. Nothing in the Tibetan or commentaries supports 'womb'.
issues.fix: within a dense mass of clouds

issues.span: occasionally / Intelligence for merit arises for a moment in the world
issues.evidence: བརྒྱ་ལམ་ན 'once in a hundred (instances/paths)' and ཐང་འགའ་འབྱུང 'only rarely arises'; bo-shenga 1-5 ཐང་འགའ་ཙམ་འབྱུང་ངོ and bo-kunpal 1-5 (བརྒྱ་ལན་རེ་སྟོང་ལན་གཉིས་ཙམ་འབྱུང 'occurs about once in a hundred or thousand times'). 'For a moment' belongs to the lightning simile (སྐད་ཅིག), not to the arising of the thought (Skt kṣaṇaṃ is not in the Tibetan line); rarity is lost.
issues.fix: once in a hundred times, the thought toward merit rarely arises in the world

1-11.translation:
Since the sole caravan leader of wandering beings, with limitless intellect,
Has thoroughly examined it and found it to be highly precious,
Those who wish to be separated from the states of wandering beings
Should firmly hold to precious bodhicitta.

issues.span: the states of wandering beings
issues.evidence: འགྲོ་བའི་གནས་ (Skt gati-pattana) refers to the realms/destinies of rebirth: bo-shenga 1-11 འགྲོ་བ་ལྔའི་གནས་ 'the abodes of the five migrations'; bo-gyaltsab 1-11 gives འཁོར་བའི་རྒུད་པ་ 'the miseries of saṃsāra'. Here འགྲོ་བ is 'migration/destiny', not 'beings', so the locked 'wandering being' misleads.
issues.fix: the realms of migration (the destinies of saṃsāra)

1-23.translation:
Whether it be a father or even a mother,
Who has such a beneficial intention?
Do even the gods or the seers,
Or does even Brahmā have this?

issues.span: Do even the gods or the seers, / Or does even Brahmā have this?
issues.evidence: Tibetan ལྷ་དང་དྲང་སྲོང་རྣམས་ཀྱང་རུང་། ("whether gods or seers") is parallel to ཕའམ་ཡང་ན་མ་ཡང་རུང་ and takes its predicate from the next line ཚངས་པ་ལ་ཡང་འདི་ཡོད་དམ། The English turns line 3 into a verbless question ("Do even the gods or the seers") and then restarts with "Or does", which is ungrammatical as it stands; bo-kunpal 1-23 reads it as gods and seers also lacking such an intention.
issues.fix:
Whether gods or seers,
Does even Brahmā have this?

1-29.translation:
For those who are destitute of happiness
And who have many sufferings,
It satisfies them with all happiness
And cuts through all suffering,

issues.span: It satisfies them with all happiness / And cuts through all suffering,
issues.evidence: The Tibetan has no pronoun subject: the verbs ཚིམ་པ་དང་། ... གཅོད་བྱེད་ཅིང་ (continued in 1-30 by སེལ་བྱེད་པ། དེ་དང་དགེ་མཚུངས་) are nominalized actions of an unstated agent, which bo-shenga 1-29 supplies as the bodhisattva (རྒྱལ་སྲས་གང་ཞིག ... བྱམས་པ་ཆེན་པོས ... སྙིང་རྗེ་ཆེན་པོས) and bo-gyaltsab 1-30 as the mind (བྱེད་ལས་ཅན་གྱི་སེམས་དེ). English "It" has no antecedent in the preceding verse (1-28 speaks of beings) and silently fixes one reading.
issues.fix:
That which satisfies them with all happiness
And cuts through all suffering,

1-33.translation:
To limitless numbers of sentient beings for a long time,
The unsurpassed happiness of the Sugatas,
Which fulfills all the wishes in their minds—
What need is there to mention constantly giving this?

issues.span: Which fulfills all the wishes in their minds— / What need is there to mention constantly giving this?
issues.evidence: In the Tibetan ཡིད་ལ་བསམ་པ་མཐའ་དག་རྫོགས་བྱེད་པ། modifies རྟག་ཏུ་སྦྱིན་པ (the constant giving), as bo-kunpal 1-33 (ཡིད་ལ་གང་ཅི་བསམ་པ་མཐའ་དག་རྫོགས་པར་བྱེད་པ་རྒྱུན་མི་འཆད་པའི་རྟག་ཏུ་སྦྱིན་པ) and Sanskrit sakalamanoratha-sampūraṇam (accusative, agreeing with the giving) show; the English relative "Which" attaches to "the unsurpassed happiness". The honor due is to the one who gives (bo-kunpal: སྦྱིན་བདག་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་རྣམས་བསྟོད་ཅིང་བཀུར་བར་འོས་པ་སྨོས་ཅི་དགོས), which "mention constantly giving this" leaves implicit.
issues.fix:
The unsurpassed happiness of the Sugatas,
Given constantly so as to fulfill all their wishes—
what need is there to mention [the honor due to one who gives thus]?

2-6.translation:
Taking them up with my mind, to the Sages, the supreme among beings,
Together with their children, I excellently offer them;
May those supreme worthy recipients of offerings, those of great compassion,
Think of me with love and accept these things of mine.

issues.span: the supreme among beings
issues.evidence: Tibetan ཐུབ་པ་སྐྱེས་ཀྱི་མཆོག; skyes bu is 'person' (not སེམས་ཅན 'beings'); bo-shenga 2-6 glosses it ཐུབ་པ་སྐྱེས་བུ་རྐང་གཉིས་རྣམས་ཀྱི་མཆོག, 'supreme among persons/bipeds', and bo-kunpal 2-6 likewise སྐྱེས་བུ་རྐང་གཉིས་མི་རྣམས་ཀྱི་མཆོག. 'Beings' is the wrong register for skyes bu and could be read as all sentient beings.
issues.fix: the supreme among persons

2-11.translation:
To the Tathāgatas and their children,
With many precious vases of scented water,
Appealing and excellently filled,
Accompanied by manifold songs and music, I offer a bath.

issues.span: Appealing and excellently filled,
issues.evidence: ཡིད་འོང་ལེགས་པར་བཀང་བ: 'filled well with (what is) pleasing'; bo-gyaltsab 2-11 reads ཡིད་དུ་འོང་བ་མེ་ཏོག་དང་བཅས་པས་ལེགས་པར་བཀང་བ and bo-shenga ཡིད་འོང་བས་ལེགས་པར་བཀང་བ, so 'pleasing' qualifies the scented water/contents, not the vases. In the English 'Appealing' dangles and reads as describing the vases.
issues.fix: Well filled with what is pleasing,

2-12.translation:
Their bodies, with matchless garments,
Clean and infused with supreme fragrance, I dry.
Then, to them, I offer excellently dyed,
Exceedingly fragrant, supreme robes.

issues.span: infused with supreme fragrance
issues.evidence: དྲི་རབ་བསྒོས་པ: རབ་ here is the intensive 'thoroughly' (Skt. pradhūpita 'well perfumed'); bo-shenga 2-12 བདུག་སྤོས་ཀྱི་དྲི་རབ་ཏུ་བསྒོས་པ, bo-gyaltsab 2-12 དྲི་ཞིམ་པོས་རབ་ཏུ་བསྒོས་པ 'thoroughly scented'. 'Supreme' is not in the Tibetan.
issues.fix: thoroughly perfumed

2-15.translation:
To the Lords of Sages, the supreme objects of offering,
With pleasing mandāra flowers and lotuses,
Blue lotuses, and all other fragrant things,
And beautifully strung, pleasing garlands, I make offerings.

issues.span: all other fragrant things
issues.evidence: ཨུཏྤལ་ལ་སོགས་དྲི་ཞིམ་ཐམས་ཅད: the 'fragrant (ones)' are flowers following མེ་ཏོག་; Skt. sugandhaiḥ kusumaiḥ; bo-gyaltsab 2-15 ཨུཏྤལ་ལ་སོགས་པ་དྲི་ཞིམ་པོ་ཐམས་ཅད་སིལ་མར་བྱས་པ, bo-shenga དྲི་ཞིམ་པོའི་རིགས་. 'Things' loses the restriction to flowers.
issues.fix: all other fragrant flowers

2-27.translation:
To those who reside in all directions,
The fully awakened Buddhas and those with bodhicitta,
Who possess great compassion,
Joining my palms, I pray:

issues.span: those with bodhicitta
issues.evidence: Here བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས is the abbreviated form of bodhisattva (Skt. bodhisattvān); bo-shenga 2-27 and bo-gyaltsab 2-27 both gloss it as བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ. The locked rendering "bodhicitta" is the mind, not the persons addressed alongside the Buddhas.
issues.fix: the bodhisattvas

2-30.translation:
To the Three Jewels,
To parents, or to teachers and others,
Through the gateway of the afflictions, with body, speech,
And mind, whatever harm I have done,

issues.span: to teachers and others
issues.evidence: བླ་མ་གཞན་དག་ལ: གཞན་དག qualifies བླ་མ ("other teachers"); Skt. gurushv anyeshu; bo-kunpal 2-30 བླ་མ་གཞན་དག, bo-gyaltsab 2-30 བསོད་ནམས་ཀྱི་ཞིང་བླ་མ་གཞན་དག. English "teachers and others" can be read as teachers plus other people.
issues.fix: or to other teachers

2-32.translation:
Without the purification of my misdeeds,
I may meet my death beforehand.
So that there is definite liberation from this,
Please protect me swiftly.

issues.span: I may meet my death beforehand
issues.evidence: སྔོན་དུ་འགུམ་པར་འགྱུར་དུ་མཆི states that death will come ("I am going to die"), not a possibility; bo-shenga 2-32 and bo-gyaltsab 2-32 read it as certain. "May" also reads like a wish. "Beforehand" is vague: before the misdeeds are purified (bo-kunpal 2-32 སྡིག་པ་བཤགས་པས་མ་བྱང་བར་སྔོན་དུ་འགུམ).
issues.fix: I will die before that happens

issues.span: from this
issues.evidence: འདི་ལས is explicitly "from this misdeed" in bo-kunpal 2-32 (སྡིག་པ་འདི་ལས) and bo-shenga 2-32 (སྡིག་པ་འདི་ལས); the English "this" has no clear referent (it could be death).
issues.fix: from these misdeeds

2-33.translation:
This Lord of Death cannot be trusted;
He does not wait for what is done or not done.
Whether sick or healthy,
No one can trust this fleeting life.

issues.span: this fleeting life
issues.evidence: གློ་བུར་ཚེ means life that ends suddenly/unexpectedly (Skt. ākasmika); bo-kunpal 2-33 གློ་བུར་ཉིད་དུ་མི་འཆི་བའི་ངེས་པ་མེད, bo-shenga 2-33 གློ་བུར་བའི་ཚེ, bo-gyaltsab 2-33 གློ་བུར་དུ་འཆི་བ. "Fleeting" means brief, not sudden or unpredictable.
issues.fix: this life, which can end suddenly

2-43.translation:
Even a person being led today
To a place where their limbs will be severed is terrified;
With a parched mouth, distressed eyes, and the like,
They appear transformed from how they were before.

issues.span: They appear transformed from how they were before.
issues.evidence: The Tibetan ends སྔ་ལས་གཞན་དུ་འགྱུར་སྣང་ན། with the conditional ན, confirmed by bo-kunpal 2-43 (…གཞན་དུ་འགྱུར་ཏེ་ཤིན་ཏུ་ཉམས་ཐག་པར་སྣང༷་ན༷།) and bo-shenga 2-43 (…འགྱུར་བར་སྣང་ན།). The verse is the protasis to 2-44 (…སྨོས་ཅི་དགོས), so the English makes it a standalone assertion and leaves 2-44's 'what need to mention' without its antecedent.
issues.fix: If they appear transformed from how they were before, (what need to mention ... [2-44])

2-44.translation:
What need to mention the utter misery
Of one seized by the messengers of Yama
With their terrifying physical forms,
And stricken by the great disease of terror?

issues.span: the great disease of terror
issues.evidence: འཇིགས་ཆེན་ནད་ = 'disease of great terror'; bo-shenga 2-44 glosses འཇིགས་པ་ཆེན་པོའི་ནད་ཀྱིས། and Sanskrit mahātrāsajvara. The English attaches 'great' to the disease rather than to the terror.
issues.fix: the disease of great terror

2-54.translation:
Even when frightened by an ordinary illness,
If one must act according to the physician's words,
Of a hundred faults, such as desire,
When constantly stricken by their disease, what need to mention?

issues.span:
Of a hundred faults, such as desire,
When constantly stricken by their disease, what need to mention?
issues.evidence: Tibetan འདོད་ཆགས་ལ་སོགས་ཉེས་པ་བརྒྱའི། ནད་ཀྱིས་རྟག་བཏབ་ = 'constantly afflicted by the disease of a hundred faults such as desire' (bo-shenga 2-54: ཉེས་པ་བརྒྱ་ཕྲག་དུ་མ་ཡི། ནད་ཀྱིས་དུས་རྟག་ཏུ་བཏབ་པ). The English fronts 'Of a hundred faults' so that it reads as the thing 'to mention', obscuring that the faults are the disease.
issues.fix: When one is constantly stricken by the disease of a hundred faults such as desire, what need to mention?

4-1.translation:
A child of the Victors, in that way,
Having firmly taken hold of bodhicitta,
Always and without wavering,
Should strive not to transgress the trainings.

issues.span: without wavering
issues.evidence: གཡེལ་བ་མེད་པར; bo-shenga 4-1 glosses it 'ལེ་ལོའི་གཡེལ་བ་མེད་པར' (without the negligence/slackness of laziness) and Sanskrit has 'atandritaḥ' (unslothful); bo-gyaltsab 4-1 'སེམས་སྐད་ཅིག་ཀྱང་གཡེལ་བ་མེད་པར'. 'Wavering' suggests irresolution, not lapse or negligence.
issues.fix: without lapse

4-4.translation:
If, having promised in that way,
I do not accomplish it through action,
By deceiving all those sentient beings,
What sort of wandering being will I become?

issues.span: what sort of wandering being will I become
issues.evidence: བདག་གི་འགྲོ་བ་ཅི་འདྲར་འགྱུར: here འགྲོ་བ is the destiny/course (Skt 'kā gatir me'), not a being; bo-gyaltsab 4-4 'བདག་གི་འགྲོ་བ་ཇི་འདྲར་འགྱུར་ཏེ། ངན་འགྲོར་འགྲོ་བ་ལས་མ་འདས་པའོ' and bo-shenga 4-4 treat it as the realm of rebirth. The locked 'wandering being' is applied mechanically and distorts the sense.
issues.fix: what will my destiny be?

4-8.translation:
For a bodhisattva, this
Is the heaviest among downfalls,
Because should it occur,
The welfare of all sentient beings is diminished.

issues.span: The welfare of all sentient beings is diminished.
issues.evidence: སེམས་ཅན་ཀུན་གྱི་དོན་ལ་དམན: the bodhisattva falls short in regard to beings' welfare; bo-kunpal 4-8 'སེམས་ཅན་མ་ལུས་པ་ཀུན་གྱི་དོན་བསྒྲུབ་པ་ལ་ནུས་པ་དམན་པར་འགྱུར་བ' and bo-gyaltsab 4-8 'གཞན་དོན་གྱི་བསམ་པ་ཉམས་པས...' show it is the bodhisattva's capacity to benefit beings that diminishes, not the beings' welfare as such.
issues.fix: one falls short in accomplishing the welfare of all sentient beings.

4-9.translation:
If anyone else, even for a single moment,
Creates an obstacle to this merit,
Since the welfare of sentient beings is diminished,
Their lower realms will be endless.

issues.span:
Creates an obstacle to this merit,
Since the welfare of sentient beings is diminished,
issues.evidence: འདིའི་བསོད་ནམས: 'this' refers to this bodhisattva (bo-shenga 4-9 'བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་འདིའི་བསོད་ནམས'; bo-gyaltsab 4-9). Line 3 (སེམས་ཅན་དོན་ལ་དམན་གྱུར་པས) is that the bodhisattva's ability to benefit beings is diminished (bo-gyaltsab 4-9 'ནུས་པ་དམན་པར་གྱུར་པར་བྱས་པས'); the English leaves the possessor of the merit and the thing diminished unclear.
issues.fix: Creates an obstacle to this bodhisattva's merit, / Since he is left falling short in the welfare of sentient beings,

4-10.translation:
Even the happiness of a single sentient being,
If destroying it leads to one's own ruin,
Limitless as the entirety of space,
What need to speak of destroying the happiness of embodied beings?

issues.span: Limitless as the entirety of space,
issues.evidence: ནམ་མཁའ་མ་ལུས་མཐའ་ཀླས་པའི་ལུས་ཅན: the embodied beings extend to the limits of all space (Skt 'aśeṣākāśaparyanta-vāsinām'; bo-gyaltsab 4-10 'ནམ་མཁའ་མ་ལུས་པའི་མཐའ་ཀླས་པའི་ལུས་ཅན'). The English turns this into a comparison ('as limitless as space') that is not in the text.
issues.fix: Embodied beings who pervade all of space to its limits,

4-19.translation:
If I have not practiced virtues,
And have accumulated misdeeds,
For even a hundred million eons,
I will not hear even the sound of the happy realms.

issues.span: a hundred million eons
issues.evidence: བསྐལ་པ་བྱེ་བ་བརྒྱ: བྱེ་བ is ten million (Skt koṭi), so བྱེ་བ་བརྒྱ (kalpakoṭiśata) is a hundred ten-millions, i.e. a billion, not a hundred million.
issues.fix: a hundred koṭis (ten millions) of eons

4-21.translation:
If even a misdeed committed in a single instant
Leads to dwelling in the Avīci hell for an eon,
Due to the misdeeds accumulated in beginningless saṃsāra,
What need is there to mention that I will not go to a happy realm?

issues.span: that I will not go
issues.evidence: The Tibetan བདག་གི་/subject is absent: "བདེ་འགྲོར་མི་འགྲོ་སྨོས་ཅི་དགོས" has no first-person subject (Shenga 4-21: "བདེ་འགྲོར་མི་འགྲོ་བ་ནི་སྨོས་ཅི་དགོས"), and the Sanskrit "kā sugatau kathā" is likewise impersonal. The English adds "I".
issues.fix: that one will not go to a happy realm

4-22.translation:
Having experienced just that much,
One will not attain liberation,
Because while experiencing it in this way,
Other misdeeds are fully generated.

issues.span: One will not attain liberation
issues.evidence: Commentaries gloss རྣམ་ཐར་མི་འགྱུར as not being freed from that suffering / the lower realms: bo-shenga 4-22 "སྡུག་བསྔལ་ལས་རྣམ་པར་ཐར་བར་མི་འགྱུར", bo-kunpal 4-22 "ངན་སོང་གི་གནས་དེ་ལས་རྣམ་པར་ཐར་པ་མི་འགྱུར". "Attain liberation" suggests final liberation.
issues.fix: One will not be liberated from it

4-28.translation:
The enemies of hatred, craving, and so forth,
Have no hands, feet, and so forth,
And are neither brave nor wise; yet how is it
That they have made me like a slave?

issues.span: The enemies of hatred, craving, and so forth
issues.evidence: Tibetan "ཞེ་སྡང་སྲེད་སོགས་དགྲ་རྣམས" means the enemies that are hatred, craving, etc. (Shenga 4-28 "ཞེ་སྡང་དང་སྲེད་པ་ལ་སོགས་པའི་དགྲ་བོ་རྣམས"; Sanskrit tṛṣṇādveṣādiśatravaḥ). "Enemies of hatred" reads as a genitive of opposition.
issues.fix: The enemies, hatred, craving, and so forth,

4-39.translation:
If even the scars inflicted by meaningless enemies
Are worn like ornaments upon the body,
For me, who perfectly strives to accomplish the great purpose,
Why should suffering be a harm?

issues.span: the scars inflicted by meaningless enemies
issues.evidence: "དོན་མེད་" qualifies the purposeless infliction of wounds, not the enemies: Gyaltsab 4-39 "དོན་མེད་པ་དགོས་པ་ཆུང་ངུའི་ཆེད་དུ་ལུས་ལ་དགྲ་ཡིས་རྨ་སྲོལ་བཏོད་པ"; Sanskrit akāraṇena riputkṣatāni.
issues.fix: the scars that enemies inflict for no meaningful purpose

4-41.translation:
Reaching the ends of space in the ten directions,
To liberate wandering beings from afflictions,
When I promised this, I myself
Was not freed from afflictions.

issues.span: Reaching the ends of space in the ten directions,
issues.evidence: The Tibetan ཕྱོགས་བཅུ་ནམ་མཁའི་མཐས་གཏུགས་པའི། is a genitive modifier of འགྲོ་བ (beings who extend to the ends of space; Skt daśadigvyomaparyanta-jagat; bo-kunpal 4-41 ནམ་མཁའི་མཐས་གཏུགས་པར་ཁྱབ་པའི་འགྲོ་བ). In the English the opening participial phrase dangles and can be read as describing the speaker or the act of liberating.
issues.fix: To liberate from afflictions the wandering beings who reach to the ends of space in the ten directions,

4-43.translation:
I shall be attached to this,
And, holding a grudge, engage in battle;
Afflictions of such a kind
Are excepted, as they destroy afflictions.

issues.span: Are excepted, as they destroy afflictions.
issues.evidence: The Tibetan ཉོན་མོངས་འཇོམས་བྱེད་མ་གཏོགས་སོ། leaves implicit what the exception is from; bo-gyaltsab 4-43 and bo-shenga 4-43 make it explicit: such seeming afflictions, being what destroys afflictions, are excepted from what is to be abandoned (སྤང་བྱར་མ་གཏོགས་སོ). English "excepted" alone does not say from what.
issues.fix: Are excepted from what is to be abandoned, since they destroy afflictions.

4-46.translation:
Afflictions, wretched afflictions, are abandoned by the eye of wisdom;
Expelled from my mind, where will they go?
Where will they dwell, to return and harm me?
It is only that I, being weak-minded, lack effort.

issues.span: are abandoned by the eye of wisdom
issues.evidence: ཤེས་རབ་མིག་གིས་སྤང་། is an exhortation/gerundive (Skt prajñādṛṣṭisādhyā "to be overcome by the eye of wisdom"); bo-shenga 4-46 has སྤང་བར་བྱ་སྟེ ("are to be abandoned"). The indicative passive states as fact what the verse prescribes.
issues.fix: are to be abandoned by the eye of wisdom

5-4.translation:
Tigers, lions, elephants, bears,
Snakes, and all enemies,
Hell guardians of the hell of sentient beings,
Sorcerers, and likewise rākṣasas—

issues.span: Hell guardians of the hell of sentient beings
issues.evidence: སེམས་ཅན་དམྱལ་བའི་སྲུང་མ is the locked "hell guardian" (Skt narakapālāḥ; bo-kunpal 5-4 explains them as Yama's agents in hell). Here སེམས་ཅན་དམྱལ་བ is simply "hell"; rendering the second locked entry inside the first produces a redundant, odd phrase.
issues.fix: Hell guardians

issues.span: Sorcerers
issues.evidence: བྱད་མ (Skt ḍākinī) is not a human sorcerer: bo-kunpal 5-4 describes it as a spirit/revenant incited by another's power (བྱད་མ་གདོན་རྦད་འདྲེ་རྦོད་གཏོང), and bo-gyaltsab 5-5 glosses བྱད་མ་མཁའ་འགྲོ་མ, harming through mantra.
issues.fix: Witches (ḍākinīs)

5-6.translation:
Thus, all fears and
Immeasurable sufferings too
Arise from the mind;
So the Speaker of Truth Himself has taught.

issues.span: So the Speaker of Truth Himself has taught.
issues.evidence: The last line (ཡང་དག་གསུང་བ་ཉིད་ཀྱིས་བསྟན།) reports the source of the claim in line 3 (བྱུང་བ་ཡིན་ནོ་ཞེས། "that they arise from the mind"); it is not a consequence. "So" suggests a conclusion drawn from the preceding lines; Skt yasmāt ... kathitam gives the reasoning as "since ... as taught".
issues.fix: as the Speaker of Truth Himself has taught.

5-7.translation:
The weapons of the hell of sentient beings,
Who intentionally created them?
Who created the burning iron ground?
From what did those masses of fire arise?

issues.span: From what did those masses of fire arise?
issues.evidence: The Tibetan text as given reads མེ་ཚོགས, which the English follows, but bo-gyaltsab 5-8 states that མེ་ཚོགས is a corrupt reading in some editions; Skt striyaḥ and the other readings (bo-gyaltsab 5-7 མོ་ཚོགས; bo-kunpal མོ་ཡི་ཚོགས; bo-shenga on the shalmali tree) mean the groups of women in hell.
issues.fix: From what did those groups of women arise? (with a note on the variant མེ་ཚོགས "masses of fire")

5-8.translation:
All such things as these
Were taught by the Sage to be the mind of misdeed.
Thus, in the three worlds,
There is no fear other than the mind.

issues.span: Were taught by the Sage to be the mind of misdeed.
issues.evidence: སྡིག་སེམས་ཡིན་པར ... གསུངས། is elliptical: the commentaries read it as arising from or caused by the mind of misdeed (Skt pāpacittasamudbhūtam; bo-kunpal 5-8 སྡིག་པ་མི་དགེ་བའི་སེམས་གོམས་པའི་དབང་གིས་བྱུང་བ; bo-shenga 5-8 སེམས་ཉིད་དེ་དག་གི་རྒྱུ་ཡིན). "To be the mind of misdeed" reads as identity.
issues.fix: Were taught by the Sage to be (products of) the mind of misdeed.

5-15.translation:
Whatever the result of generating a single clear mind,
Such as Brahmā and so forth,
The result of body and speech, too,
Because of weak conduct, is not like that.

issues.span: The result of body and speech, too,
issues.evidence: Tibetan ལུས་ངག་བཅས་པའི་འབྲས་བུ་ཡང་ = the result [of effort] 'accompanied by' body and speech, even so. Sanskrit sahāpi vākśarīrābhyām ('even together with speech and body'); bo-kunpal 5-15 ལུས་ངག་དང་བཅས་པའི་འབད་རྩོལ་ཆེན་པོས; bo-gyaltsab 5-15 ལུས་ངག་དང་བཅས་པའི་སེམས་ཀྱི་འབྲས་བུ་ཡང༌། The English drops བཅས་པ ('together with') and so reads body and speech alone as the source.
issues.fix: The result, even when accompanied by body and speech,

5-32.translation:
Having thought in this way, with shame,
Respect, and fear, one should bear it in mind.
Therefore, the recollection of the Buddha
Will also arise in one again and again.

issues.span: one should bear it in mind
issues.evidence: དེ་བཞིན་གནོས (mnos) is "undertake/take on likewise"; bo-kunpal 5-32 glosses དེ་བཞིན་དུ་མནོས་ཏེ་གནས་པར་གྱིས་ཤིག ("having so undertaken, remain"), Sanskrit tathā tiṣṭhet "remain thus". "Bear it in mind" adds an object ("it") and drops the དེ་བཞིན "thus/likewise" that links back to the shame, respect and fear.
issues.fix: one should thus take it on and remain so

5-34.translation:
First, having recognized a mind such as this
To be faulty,
At that time I, like a piece of wood,
Should remain steadfast.

issues.span: like a piece of wood
issues.evidence: ཤིང་བཞིན་ is rendered "like a log of wood" in the glossary and in 5-48, 5-50, 5-51; here the same phrase ཤིང་བཞིན་དུ་ཡང་ is rendered "like a piece of wood", an unmotivated inconsistency (bo-kunpal 5-34 likens it to a great tree stump unmoved by wind).
issues.fix: like a log of wood

5-39.translation:
Having prepared for an action with the thought,
"My body shall remain like this,"
One should then occasionally look,
Asking, "How is this body remaining?"

issues.span: Having prepared for an action
issues.evidence: བྱ་བ་བསྡོགས་ནས is glossed by bo-shenga 5-39 as བརྩམས་པར་བྱས་ནས ("having begun/set about") and by bo-kunpal 5-39 as བྱ་བ་དེའི་མགོ་བརྩམས་པ ("having begun that action"); Sanskrit kriyām ākṣipya. The action is already started, not merely prepared for.
issues.fix: Having set about an action with the thought,

5-40.translation:
So that the mad elephant of the mind
Does not escape from how it is bound
To the great pillar of reflecting on the Dharma,
One should examine with all effort.

issues.span: Does not escape from how it is bound
issues.evidence: ཇི་ལྟར་བཏགས་པ་མི་འཆོར་བར། དེ་ལྟར་འབད་པ་ཀུན་གྱིས་བརྟག is a ji-ltar...de-ltar clause: as bound, it does not escape (bo-gyaltsab 5-40: ཇི་ལྟར་བཏགས་པ་མི་འཆོར་བར་). "Escape from how it is bound" is hard to parse and suggests escaping a manner of binding, not escaping the pillar.
issues.fix: So that the mad elephant of the mind, once tied to the great pillar of reflecting on the Dharma, does not escape

5-46.translation:
If one digs the earth or cuts grass without purpose,
Or draws lines on the ground and so forth,
Having remembered the training of the Sugatas,
One should, out of fear, instantly abandon them.

issues.span: the training of the Sugatas
issues.evidence: བདེ་གཤེགས་བསླབ་པ has no plural marker; bo-gyaltsab 5-46 has བདེ་གཤེགས་ཀྱི་བསླབ་པ and bo-shenga བདེ་བར་གཤེགས་པའི་བསླབ་པ (singular); Sanskrit tāthāgatīṃ śikṣām is singular.
issues.fix: the training of the Sugata

5-52.translation:
Forsaking the welfare of others,
And desiring to pursue my own welfare,
Or if a mind desiring to speak arises,
Then I should remain like a log of wood.

issues.span: Forsaking the welfare of others, / And desiring to pursue my own welfare, / Or if a mind desiring to speak arises
issues.evidence: Tibetan: གཞན་དོན་ཡལ་བར་འདོར་བ་དང་། རང་དོན་གཉེར་བར་འདོད་པ་དང་། སྨྲ་བར་འདོད་པའི་སེམས་བྱུང་ན། — three parallel items joined by དང་ all governed by one སེམས་བྱུང་ན ("if a mind ... arises"); bo-gyaltsab 5-52: ཡལ་བར་འདོར་བའམ། རང་དོན་གཉེར་བར་འདོད་པ་དག་དང་། ངག་སྨྲ་བར་འདོད་པའི་སེམས་བྱུང་ན. The English leaves "Forsaking" and "desiring" as dangling participles with no subject and switches to "Or if" for the last item, so the syntax of the three clauses is unclear.
issues.fix: If a mind arises that forsakes the welfare of others, desires to pursue my own welfare, or desires to speak,

5-56.translation:
Do not be disheartened by the mutually discordant
Desires of childish ones,
But thinking, "Due to the arising of their afflictions,
This mind has arisen," be a compassionate one.

issues.span: Due to the arising of their afflictions, / This mind has arisen
issues.evidence: Tibetan: ཉོན་མོངས་སྐྱེས་པ་འདི་དག་གི། སེམས་འདི་བྱུང་སྙམ — the genitive འདི་དག་གི ("of these [beings]") governs སེམས་འདི ("this mind"); bo-gyaltsab 5-56: འདི་དག་གི་སེམས་འདི་བྱུང་བས; bo-kunpal: བྱིས་པ་འདི་དག་གི་ ... སེམས་འདི་ལྟ་བུ་ ... བྱུང་བའོ་སྙམ. In the English "their" modifies only "afflictions", so "this mind" could be read as the practitioner's own mind.
issues.fix: "Because afflictions have arisen in them, this mind of theirs has arisen,"

5-59.translation:
By vultures craving flesh,
Even when dragged back and forth everywhere,
If you, O mind, are not displeased,
Why do you care for it now?

issues.span: Even when dragged back and forth everywhere ... Why do you care for it now?
issues.evidence: The Tibetan elides the object (the corpse/body); bo-shenga 5-59 and bo-gyaltsab 5-59 supply it: ལུས་དེ་ ... བཤལ་ཅིང་ཁྲིད་ཀྱང་ ... ལུས་ལ་ཆགས་ནས་ཁ་ཏ་བྱེད. The English gives no antecedent for the dragged thing or for "it", and the preceding verse (5-58) concerns the mind, so "it" is likely to be misread.
issues.fix: Even when [the body] is dragged back and forth everywhere ... Why do you now care for [it]?

5-78.translation:
In this, there is no loss for me here,
And in the next life there is great happiness.
Through faults, there is unhappiness and suffering,
And in the next life there is great suffering.

issues.span: In this, there is no loss for me here,
issues.evidence: བདག་ལ་འདིར་གོད་ཡོང་མེད་ལ། འདིར = 'here, in this life', contrasted with ཕ་རོལ་དུ (next life); bo-shenga 5-78 ཚེ་འདིར་གོད་པར་འགྱུར་བ་ཡོང་མེད; bo-kunpal 5-78 ཚེ་འདིར. 'In this ... here' is redundant and leaves 'this' unspecified.
issues.fix: In this life there is no loss for me,

5-81.translation:
Whether motivated by constant strong dedication
Or motivated by an antidote,
Toward the fields of good qualities and benefactors,
And those who are suffering, virtue becomes great.

issues.span: strong dedication
issues.evidence: མངོན་ཞེན་ = intense fixation/zeal; bo-kunpal 5-81 glosses it as འདུན་པ་ཤུགས་དྲག་པོ (powerful aspiration, e.g. from faith and compassion); bo-gyaltsab 5-81 འདུན་པ་དྲག་པོས་བྱ་བ. 'Dedication' suggests dedication of merit (བསྔོ་བ).
issues.fix: intense, fixed aspiration

5-85.translation:
One should share with those fallen into ruin, the unprotected,
And those established in ascetic discipline;
One should eat only a moderate amount,
And give away everything except the three Dharma robes.

issues.span: those fallen into ruin
issues.evidence: ལོག་པར་ལྟུང་ = fallen into wrong/lower states; bo-kunpal 5-85 ལོག་པར་ལྟུང་བ་བྱ་ཁྱི་ལ་སོགས་པ་དུད་འགྲོ་; bo-gyaltsab 5-85 adds animals and pretas (དུད་འགྲོ་དང་ཡི་དྭགས). 'Ruin' could be read as worldly (e.g. financial) ruin.
issues.fix: those fallen into wretched states (animals and the like)

5-89.translation:
Do not teach the profound and vast to the lesser,
Nor to a woman without a man present;
Toward the lesser and supreme Dharmas,
One should always act with equal respect.

issues.span: to the lesser
issues.evidence: དམན་ལ་ = to those of lesser capacity/inclination. bo-kunpal 5-89 བློ་དམན་པ་ཉན་རང་གི་ལམ་ལ་མོས་པ; bo-gyaltsab 5-89 བསམ་པ་དམན་པ. The same word 'lesser' then modifies Dharmas in line 3, so the English blurs persons and teachings.
issues.fix: to those of lesser capacity

5-90.translation:
Those who have become vessels for the vast Dharma
Should not be engaged in the lesser Dharma;
Conduct should not be completely forsaken,
Nor should they be deceived with sūtras and mantras.

issues.span: Nor should they be deceived with sūtras and mantras.
issues.evidence: མདོ་དང་སྔགས་ཀྱིས་འདྲིད་མི་བྱ་: the agent is the teacher, who should not lure others (into neglecting conduct) with sūtras and mantras. bo-gyaltsab 5-90 མདོ་དང་སྔགས་ཀྱིས་གཞན་འདྲིད་པར་མི་བྱའོ; bo-shenga 5-90 ... ཁྱོད་དག་པར་འགྱུར་རོ་ཞེས་འདྲིད་པར་མི་བྱ. The English passive leaves the agent unstated and 'deceived' misses 'lure/entice'.
issues.fix: nor should one lure them with sūtras and mantras.

issues.span: wave the arms excessively
issues.evidence: Tibetan ལག་པ་ཤས་ཆེར་བསྐྱོད་མིན་ཏེ has ལག་པ (hand), not arm; bo-shenga 5-95 and bo-gyaltsab 5-95 likewise speak of hands (ལག་པ), the context being small gestures when handing things over.
issues.fix: One should not move the hands excessively

5-97.translation:
Although the conduct of the bodhisattva for awakening
Is taught to be measureless,
One should certainly practice
The conduct of purifying the mind for that long.

issues.span: the bodhisattva for awakening
issues.evidence: བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའི་སྤྱོད་པ་ is rendered with the locked "conduct of the bodhisattva"; བྱང་ཆུབ་ is part of the word བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ (bodhisattva), and no separate "for awakening" is in the Tibetan.
issues.fix: Although the conduct of bodhisattvas

issues.span: for that long
issues.evidence: དེ་སྲིད་ is correlative: bo-shenga 5-97 specifies the span as ངེས་པར་བློ་མ་འབྱུང་གི་བར་དེ་སྲིད་དུ and bo-gyaltsab 5-97 as ངེས་པར་སྤྱོད་པ་མཐའ་དག་ཉམས་སུ་ལེན་ནུས་པ་དེ་སྲིད་, i.e. until one is able to practice all of it. "For that long" has no antecedent in the English.
issues.fix: for as long as one is unable to practice it all (until one can do so)

5-98.translation:
Three times by day and three times by night,
One should recite the Three Heaps Sūtra;
By relying on the Victor and the bodhicitta of awakening,
One should thereby pacify the remaining downfalls.

issues.span: the bodhicitta of awakening
issues.evidence: བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་ is locked as "bodhicitta"; "of awakening" duplicates the བྱང་ཆུབ་ already contained in the term (bo-shenga 5-98: རང་གི་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཀྱི་སེམས).
issues.fix: the Victor and bodhicitta

5-100.translation:
That which is not a training for the children of the Victors
Does not exist at all;
For the wise who abide in this way,
There is nothing that does not become merit.

issues.span: That which is not a training for the children of the Victors Does not exist at all
issues.evidence: Tibetan རྒྱལ་སྲས་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་མི་བསླབ་པ། དེ་ནི་གང་ཡང་ཡོད་མིན: the agent is the Victors' children (ཀྱིས) and the verb is བསླབ (train in): nothing exists that they do not train in. Sanskrit yan na śikṣyaṃ jinātmajaiḥ; bo-shenga 5-100: རིག་པའི་གནས་ཀུན་ལ་མི་བསླབ་པ། དེ་ནི་གང་ཡང་ཡོད་པ་མིན.
issues.fix: There is nothing at all that the children of the Victors do not train in

6-2.translation:
There is no misdeed like hatred;
There is no austerity like patience.
Therefore, earnestly upon patience,
One should practice meditation in various ways.

issues.span:
Therefore, earnestly upon patience,
One should practice meditation in various ways.
issues.evidence: བཟོད་ལ་ནན་ཏན་དུ། སྣ་ཚོགས་ཚུལ་དུ་བསྒོམ་པར་བྱ། ("meditate on patience earnestly in various ways"; bo-kunpal 6-2: བཟོད་པ་བསྒོམ་པ་ལ་ནན་ཏན་དུ་བྱས་ཏེ). The English splits "patience" from the verb "practice meditation", leaving "earnestly upon patience" a dangling phrase that is hard to parse.
issues.fix: Therefore, one should earnestly meditate on patience in various ways.

6-11.translation:
For myself or for my friends,
Suffering, contempt, harsh words,
And disrepute are not desired;
For an enemy, it is the opposite.

issues.span: For an enemy, it is the opposite.
issues.evidence: དགྲ་ལ་དེ་ལས་བཟློག་པས་སོ། ends with the reason particle པས་སོ ("because for an enemy it is the reverse of that"); bo-gyaltsab 6-11 ties the reversal of wanting/not-wanting to the enemy as the reason. The English drops the causal link and leaves "it" vague.
issues.fix: because, for an enemy, these are the reverse (what is wanted rather than unwanted).

6-13.translation:
Devotees of Durgā and the Karṇapas
Endure the feeling of burning, cutting, and so forth
Pointlessly; for the sake of liberation,
Why then am I cowardly?

issues.span: Why then am I cowardly?
issues.evidence: བདག་གོ་ཅི་ཕྱིར་སྔར། has no word for "coward" (the Sanskrit kātaraḥ does). bo-kunpal 6-13 glosses it as "why is it not fitting for me to endure" (ཅི་ཡིས་ཕྱིར་སྔར་ཏེ་སྔར་མི་རིགས་སོ), and bo-gyaltsab 6-13 as "why should I not endure it" (བདག་ཀོ་ཅི་ཞིག་བསྟར་ཏེ་བཟོད་པར་རིགས་སོ).
issues.fix: why should I not endure it?

6-21.translation:
Furthermore, the good quality of suffering is:
Through sorrow, haughtiness is dispelled,
Compassion arises for those in saṃsāra,
One shuns misdeeds and delights in virtue.

issues.span: Through sorrow
issues.evidence: སྐྱོ་བས is weariness or disenchantment with saṃsāra (Sanskrit saṃvega), not grief: bo-shenga 6-21 སེམས་སྐྱོ་བར་གྱུར་པས; bo-kunpal 6-21 ཡིད་འབྱུང་ཞིང་སྐྱོ་བར་གྱུར་པས ("becoming weary, disenchanted"). "Sorrow" suggests grief.
issues.fix: Through disillusionment (weariness with saṃsāra)

6-24.translation:
Even without thinking, "I shall become angry,"
People become angry spontaneously;
Even without thinking, "I shall produce it,"
Anger likewise arises.

issues.span: People become angry spontaneously
issues.evidence: སྐྱེ་བོ་རྣམས་ནི་གྱི་ནར་ཁྲོ། (gyi nar = on whatever slight condition happens along). bo-kunpal 6-24: 'རྐྱེན་ཕལ་པ་ཙམ་ལ་བརྟེན་ནས་ཁྲོ་བར་འགྱུར' (becomes angry depending on a mere ordinary condition); bo-shenga 6-24: 'རྐྱེན་ཇི་ནར་ཙམ་གྱིས'. 'Spontaneously' can read as uncaused, which the passage's argument (all arises from conditions) excludes.
issues.fix: People become angry at the slightest condition

6-30.translation:
If, even at the time of acting, it remains as before,
What has the action done to it?
In saying, "This is its action,"
What connection could there be?

issues.span: In saying, "This is its action," What connection could there be?
issues.evidence: དེ་ཡི་བྱེད་པ་འདི་ཡིན་ཞེས། འབྲེལ་པར་འགྱུར་བ་གང་ཞིག་ཡོད། asks what relation exists by which one could say 'this is its action'; bo-gyaltsab 6-30: 'བདག་དེའི་... བྱེད་པ་འདི་ཡིན་ཞེས་བདག་དང་འབྲེལ་བར་འགྱུར་བ་གང་ཞིག་ཡོད'. 'In saying' wrongly suggests the connection lies in the act of saying.
issues.fix: What connection could there be by which one could say, "This is its action"?

6-31.translation:
Thus, everything is under the power of others,
And through that power, it is powerless.
Knowing this, one will not become angry
At any entities, which are like emanations.

issues.span: which are like emanations
issues.evidence: The Tibetan as given reads སྦྲུལ་ལྟ་བུའི ('snake-like'), also in bo-shenga 6-31 (སྦྲུལ་ལྟ་བུའི་རང་བཞིན), whereas the Sanskrit has nirmāṇavat and bo-kunpal/bo-gyaltsab 6-31 read སྤྲུལ་པ་ལྟ་བུ / སྤྲུལ་ལྟ་བུ (emanation). The English follows the Sanskrit and commentaries, not the Tibetan wording; the divergence should be flagged for the reader.
issues.fix: which are like emanations [the Tibetan text here reads sbrul, 'snake', likely a scribal error for sprul]

6-35.translation:
Through heedlessness, they even harm themselves
With thorns and so forth;
In order to obtain women and the like,
They become obsessed and engage in fasting and so forth.

issues.span: they become obsessed
issues.evidence: རྔམ་ཞིང (vehement, fierce, in a fervor). Sanskrit has kopāt ('out of anger'); bo-gyaltsab 6-35 'རྔམ་ཞིང་ཁྲོས་པས' (fierce and angry), bo-kunpal 'རྔམ་ཞིང་ཆགས་ནས', bo-shenga 'བརྣབ་སེམས་ཀྱིས་རྔམ་ཞིང'. 'Obsessed' loses the sense of fierce vehemence/anger.
issues.fix: they grow vehement (in fury)

6-38.translation:
When, through the arising of afflictions,
They engage in such acts as killing themselves,
If compassion does not even arise,
What point is there in feeling anger?

issues.span: When, through the arising of afflictions, They engage in such acts as killing themselves, If compassion does not even arise,
issues.evidence: བདག་གསོད་ལ་སོགས་ཞུགས་པ་ལ། སྙིང་རྗེ་རྒྱ་ལ་མ་སྐྱེས་ན། — compassion fails to arise toward ('ལ') those who engage in self-harm (bo-gyaltsab 6-38: 'བདག་གསོད་པ་ལ་སོགས་པ་ལ་ཞུགས་པ་ལ་སྙིང་རྗེ་བྱ་བར་འོས'). The English 'When ... they engage' leaves the object of compassion unstated and parses as two unrelated clauses.
issues.fix: For those who, through the arising of afflictions, engage in such acts as killing themselves, if compassion does not even arise [toward them], what sense is there in anger?

6-41.translation:
While sticks and the like are directly employed,
If I feel anger toward the one who wields them,
Since they too are impelled by hatred,
If anything, it is appropriate to feel anger at hatred.

issues.span: If I feel anger
issues.evidence: གལ་ཏེ་འཕེན་པ་ལ་ཁྲོ་ན། has no first-person subject; bo-gyaltsab 6-41 treats it as impersonal ('གལ་ཏེ་འཕེན་པར་བྱེད་པ་ལ་ཁྲོ་ན'). The Sanskrit has kupyate (passive/impersonal).
issues.fix: if one feels anger

issues.span: While sticks and the like are directly employed,
issues.evidence: དབྱུག་པ་ལ་སོགས་དངོས་བཀོལ་ཏེ། — sticks etc. are the actual instruments (dngos) the person employs; bo-shenga 6-41: 'དབྱུག་པ་ལ་སོགས་པའི་དངོས་པོ་རྣམས་བཀོལ་ཏེ་ལུས་ལ་བརྡེག་པ་ན' (having employed sticks etc., when they strike the body). 'While ... directly employed' is a confusing temporal/concessive rendering. Also 'ཉིས་ན' (bo-shenga: 'གཅིག་ཏུ... ཉེས་ན་སྟེ་གཉིས་སུ་ན', 'firstly the sticks; secondly, hatred') is rendered as 'If anything'.
issues.fix: Having employed sticks and the like as the actual instruments, if one is angry at the one who throws them, since he too is driven by hatred, then, in the second place, it is fitting to be angry at hatred.

6-43.translation:
His weapon and my body,
Both are causes of suffering;
Since he produced the weapon and I the body,
At whom should I direct my anger?

issues.span: Since he produced the weapon and I the body
issues.evidence: Tibetan ཕྱུང་ (དེས་མཚོན་བདག་གི་ལུས་ཕྱུང་ན) means drew out/brought forth; bo-shenga 6-43 glosses "དགྲ་བོ་དེས་མཚོན་ཕྱུང་ཞིང་བདག་གིས་ལུས་ཕྱུང་ན", bo-kunpal "མཚོན་ཆ་ཕྱུངས་ཤིང་... ལུས་ཕྱུང་ནས". Sanskrit gṛhīta "taken up". "Produced" implies creation, not drawing out/taking up.
issues.fix: Since he has drawn the weapon and I have taken up the body,

6-45.translation:
Childish ones do not desire suffering,
Yet they crave the causes of suffering;
When harmed by their own faults,
Why should they resent others?

issues.span: Why should they resent others?
issues.evidence: Tibetan གཞན་ལ་བཀོན་དུ་ཅི་ཞིག་ཡོད། — བཀོན་ is "to blame/lay the fault on" (bo-kunpal: "གཞན་ལ་ཁྲོ་ཞིང་བཀོན་དུ་ཅི་ཞིག་ཡོད"; bo-shenga "གཞན་དགྲ་བོ་དག་ལ་བཀོན་ཏུ་ཅི་ཞིག་ཡོད"), not inner resentment; also the Tibetan is "what is there to blame on others", a statement of there being no basis.
issues.fix: what grounds are there to blame others?

6-66.translation:
To embodied beings, beings with a mind
And the insentient both cause harm;
Why single out beings with a mind for resentment?
Therefore, practice patience toward harm.

issues.span:
To embodied beings, beings with a mind
And the insentient both cause harm;
issues.evidence: ལུས་ཅན་རྣམས་ལ་སེམས་ཡོད་དང་། སེམས་མེད་གཉི་གས་གནོད་བྱས་ན། — 'embodied beings' are the recipients of harm; 'sentient' (སེམས་ཡོད) and 'insentient' (སེམས་མེད) are the two agents (bo-shenga 6-66: སེམས་ཅན་རྣམས་ལ་སེམས་ཡོད་པའི་འགྲོ་བ་དང་སེམས་མེད་པའི་ནད་ལ་སོགས་པ་གཉིས་ཀས་གནོད་པར་བྱས་ན). The English comma lets 'beings with a mind' read in apposition to 'embodied beings'.
issues.fix:
If both beings with a mind
and the insentient cause harm to embodied beings;

6-71.translation:
Likewise, whatever the mind has attachment to,
Causing the fire of hatred to spread,
Out of fear that merit will be burned,
That must be discarded instantly.

issues.span:
whatever the mind has attachment to,
Causing the fire of hatred to spread,
issues.evidence: གང་ལ་སེམས་ཆགས་ནས། ཞེ་སྡང་མེ་ནི་མཆེད་གྱུར་པ། — the fire of hatred has spread (intransitive, མཆེད་གྱུར་པ) onto the object of attachment (bo-gyaltsab 6-71: ཆགས་པའི་གཞི་དེ་ནི...). The dangling participle 'Causing' obscures what causes what.
issues.fix: whatever the mind is attached to, in which the fire of hatred has spread,

6-78.translation:
Thinking, "In that way, the other will be happy,"
If you do not desire this happiness,
Through forsaking the giving of wages and the like,
The seen and unseen will be ruined.

issues.evidence: The line begins གཞན་ཡང་དེ་ལྟར་བདེ་འགྱུར་ཞེས། ('Moreover / Furthermore'); the English drops གཞན་ཡང་, which marks this as a further argument (bo-gyaltsab 6-78 repeats གཞན་ཡང་).
issues.fix: Moreover, thinking, "In that way, the other will be happy,"

6-82.translation:
Whoever is a dependent you nurture,
To whom you yourself must give,
If those relatives find a livelihood,
Will you not be glad, but instead become angry?

issues.span: Will you not be glad, but instead become angry?
issues.evidence: དགར་མི་འགྱུར་བར་སླར་ཁྲོའམ། is "instead of being glad, do you (rather) get angry?" (bo-shenga 6-82: དགའ་བར་མི་འགྱུར་བར་སླར་དེ་ལ་ཁྲོའམ་ཅི། ; Skt na hṛṣyasi prakupyasi). The English "Will you not be glad" can be read as asking whether you will be glad.
issues.fix: Instead of being glad, do you become angry in return?

6-85.translation:
Merit and faith,
Or your own good qualities, why do you cast them away?
Not taking hold of the gains that occur,
Tell me, why do you not become angry?

issues.span: Not taking hold of the gains that occur,
issues.evidence: རྙེད་པ་གྱུར་པ་མི་འཛིན་པ། is explained as not holding the causes that bring gain (bo-kunpal 6-85: རྙེད་པ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་ཐོབ་པར་གྱུར་པ་ཡི་རྒྱུ་དེ་དག་མི་འཛིན་པ; bo-gyaltsab: རྙེད་པ་ཐོབ་པར་འགྱུར་བའི་རྒྱུ་མི་འཛིན་པ). The English reads as failing to take gains already received; also the object of the anger (oneself) is left unstated (bo-gyaltsab: ཁྲོ་ན་རང་ཉིད་ལ་ཁྲོ་བར་རིགས་སོ།).
issues.fix: Not holding on to what would bring you gains, tell me, why are you not angry at yourself?

6-89.translation:
Cast by the fisherman of the afflictions,
This hook is an unbearable barb;
Caught by it, in the cauldrons of hell,
The hell guardians will certainly boil me.

issues.span: an unbearable barb
issues.evidence: མི་བཟད་གཟེ། means unbearable and fierce/terrible (bo-kunpal: གཟེ་བའམ་རྣོ་བ; bo-shenga: འཇིགས་པའི་གནས་ཡིན་པས་མི་བཟད་པར་གཟེ་བ; Skt ghora). "Barb" is not what གཟེ conveys and "hook ... barb" is redundant.
issues.fix: is unbearable and terrible

6-94.translation:
First of all, since sound is mindless,
It cannot possibly have the intention to praise me.
As for the renown that "Others are pleased with me,"
Perhaps that is the cause of joy?

issues.span: the renown that "Others are pleased with me,"
issues.evidence: བདག་ལ་གཞན་དགའ་ཞེས་གྲགས་པ། here grags pa is "being said/known" that another is pleased (bo-shenga 6-94: བདག་ལ་གཞན་བསྟོད་པར་བྱེད་པ་དེ་དགའ་བ་ཡིན་ཞེས་གྲགས་པ), not "renown" in the sense of fame (the glossary sense of གྲགས་པ).
issues.fix: the fact that it is said, "Others are pleased with me,"

6-114.translation:
It is not by the good quality of intention itself,
But it is from the result that they are similar.
Sentient beings too possess good qualities,
And therefore they are equal.

issues.span:
But it is from the result that they are similar.
Sentient beings too possess good qualities,
issues.evidence: Tibetan འབྲས་བུ་ལས་ཡིན་དེས་མཚུངས་པར། སེམས་ཅན་རྣམས་ལའང་ཡོན་ཏན་ཡོད། has དེས་མཚུངས་པར 'just as [the Buddhas]' (Kunpal 6-114: སངས་རྒྱས་རྣམས་དང་མཚུངས་པར་སེམས་ཅན་རྣམས་ལའང་ཡོན་ཏན་ཡོད), which the English drops; 'they' in line 2 has no stated referent (Buddhas and sentient beings, as fields; Gyaltsab 6-114).
issues.fix: But it is from the result that [the two] are alike. Just like the Buddhas, sentient beings too possess good qualities,

6-116.translation:
Because they have a share in accomplishing the qualities of a Buddha,
They are therefore asserted to be equal.
Yet to those with an infinite ocean of good qualities,
To the Buddhas, no one is equal.

issues.span: They are therefore asserted to be equal.
issues.evidence: Tibetan དེས་ན་དེ་དག་མཉམ་པར་འདོད 'therefore those two [sentient beings and Buddhas] are held to be equal'. Kunpal 6-116: སེམས་ཅན་དང་སངས་རྒྱས་དེ་དག་མཉམ་པར་འདོད; Sanskrit sattvā jinaiḥ samāḥ. English 'They' has no stated counterpart, so the equality is not tied to sentient beings and the Buddhas.
issues.fix: Therefore sentient beings and the Buddhas are held to be equal.

7-4.translation:
Having been snared by the fowler of the afflictions,
Having been caught in the net of birth,
And having gone into the mouth of the Lord of Death,
How is it that you still do not know?

issues.span: Having been snared by the fowler of the afflictions
issues.evidence: ཉོན་མོངས་རྒྱ་པས་བཤོར་ནས། bshor = driven/chased (bo-kunpal 7-4: བཤོར་བའམ་དེད་ནས; bo-shenga: བཤོར་ཏེ་དབང་དུ་བྱས་ནས); the net (རྒྱ) is the next line's image; bo-gyaltsab glosses རྒྱ་བ as རྔོན་པ་ 'hunter'. 'Snared' pre-empts the net image.
issues.fix: Having been driven down by the hunter of the afflictions,

7-5.translation:
That your own group is being killed one by one,
Have you not seen this?
Yet whoever relies on sleep
Is like an outcaste and a buffalo.

issues.span:
Yet whoever relies on sleep
Is like an outcaste and a buffalo.
issues.evidence: གཉིད་ལ་བརྟེན་པ་གང་། གདོལ་པ་དང་ནི་མ་ཧེ་བཞིན། is addressed to the same 'you' (ཁྱོད). All three commentaries read the comparison as the buffalo that sleeps unafraid while the outcaste kills others (bo-gyaltsab 7-5: གདོལ་བས་... གསོད་པའི་མ་ཧེ; bo-shenga: གདོལ་པ་དང་ནི་བསད་པར་བྱ་བའི་མ་ཧེ). English can be read as comparing the sleeper to both an outcaste and a buffalo.
issues.fix:
Yet you who rely on sleep
Are like a buffalo beside its outcaste butcher.

7-12.translation:
When touched by hot water,
It is intensely hot for one with tender flesh;
Having created the karma of hell,
Why do you remain at ease like this?

issues.span: It is intensely hot for one with tender flesh;
issues.evidence: The Tibetan 'ཆུ་ཚན་གྱིས་ནི་རེག་པ་ན། གཞོན་ཤ་ཅན་ལ་རབ་ཚ་བའི།' is addressed to the listener (Sanskrit 'sukumāra pratapyase', 'you of tender body are scorched'); bo-gyaltsab 7-12 says the body of tender flesh must experience intensely hot suffering. The English line 2 introduces an impersonal 'It' and a generic 'one', losing the addressee.
issues.fix: When touched by hot water, you of tender flesh are intensely scorched;

7-22.translation:
The suffering of my accomplishing awakening
Has a limit;
To remove the harm of a splinter destroying from within,
It is like the suffering of making a cut in the body.

issues.span:
To remove the harm of a splinter destroying from within,
It is like the suffering of making a cut in the body.
issues.evidence: The Tibetan 'ཟུག་རྔུ་ཁོང་བརླག་གནོད་བསལ་ཕྱིར། ལུས་རྨ་བཏོད་པའི་སྡུག་བསྔལ་བཞིན།' makes the purpose clause qualify the cutting (Sanskrit 'naṣṭaśalyavyathāpohe tad-utpādana-duḥkhavat'); bo-shenga 7-22: 'ཟུག་རྔུ་ཁོང་བརླག་གི་གནོད་པ་བསལ་བའི་ཕྱིར། ལུས་ལ་རྨ་བཏོད་ནས...'. The English has a dangling infinitive and an unclear 'It'.
issues.fix: It is just like the suffering of cutting open the body in order to remove the harm of a splinter that is destroying it from within.

7-29.translation:
Because this, through the power of bodhicitta,
Exhausts previous misdeeds
And gathers an ocean of merit,
It is explained to be superior to the Śrāvakas.

issues.span: Because this,
issues.evidence: Tibetan འདི་ནི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་སྟོབས་ཀྱིས། — 'this' is the bodhisattva (bo-kunpal 7-29 བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་འདི་ནི; bo-gyaltsab 7-29 སྙིང་རྗེ་ཅན་འདི་ནི). English 'this' has no antecedent.
issues.fix: Because this [bodhisattva], through the power of bodhicitta,

7-31.translation:
To accomplish the welfare of sentient beings, the forces
Are aspiration, steadfastness, joy, and relinquishment.
Aspiration is generated through the fear of suffering
And by contemplating its benefits.

issues.span: contemplating its benefits
issues.evidence: དེ་ཡི་ཕན་ཡོན་ — 'its' is not clear after 'suffering'; bo-shenga 7-31 glosses དགེ་བ་ལ་གོམས་པ་དེ་ཡི་ཕན་ཡོན (benefits of virtue/aspiration), bo-kunpal 7-31 མོས་པ་དེ་ཡི་ཕན་ཡོན (benefits of that aspiration). English 'its' could be read as suffering's benefits.
issues.fix: contemplating the benefits of that aspiration

7-37.translation:
I have not made offerings to the Blessed One,
Nor provided the happiness of great festivals;
I have not performed service for the teaching,
Nor fulfilled the wishes of the poor.

issues.span: great festivals
issues.evidence: དགའ་སྟོན་ཆེན་པོ་ is singular 'great feast/festival' (Skt mahotsava); bo-shenga 7-37 glosses it as the Sangha's great feast (དགེ་འདུན་ཀྱི་ཚོགས་ཀྱི་དགའ་སྟོན་ཆེན་པོ). English pluralizes.
issues.fix: the great festival

7-48.translation:
Habituated to that in any other life,
misdeeds and suffering will increase.
Any other deed and the time of the result
will become inferior, and that too will not be accomplished.

issues.span:
Any other deed and the time of the result
will become inferior
issues.evidence: Tibetan 'གཞན་དང་འབྲས་བུའི་དུས་ཀྱང་ནི། དམན་འགྱུར་དེ་ཡང་འགྲུབ་མི་འགྱུར།'; bo-gyaltsab 7-48 reads 'ཕྱིས་བརྩམས་པའི་བྱ་བ་གཞན་དང་ ... འབྲས་བུའི་དུས་ཀྱང་ནི་དམན་པར་འགྱུར་བ་དུས་རིང་བོར་འགོར་བ་དང་། ལས་གཞན་དེ་ཡང་འགྲུབ་པར་མི་འགྱུར' (a later-begun other action; the result's timing is degraded/delayed; that other action is not accomplished). 'Any' is not in the Tibetan, and the English does not make clear which item becomes inferior or what 'that' refers to.
issues.fix: Another deed, and the time of the result, will become inferior, and that other deed too will not be accomplished.

7-62.translation:
Just as one desires the joyful result of play,
Whatever is the action to be done,
One should be attached to that action,
And, unsated by that action, find joy in it.

issues.span: Whatever is the action to be done,
issues.evidence: 'འདི་ཡིས་བྱ་བའི་ལས་གང་ཡིན།' - 'འདི་ཡིས' (by this one, i.e. the bodhisattva) is unrendered; bo-gyaltsab 7-62 'བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་འདི་ཡིས་གཞན་དོན་བྱ་བའི་ལས་གང་ཡིན་པའི་ལས་'; bo-shenga 7-62 'བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་འདི་ཡི་བྱ་བའི་ལས་'.
issues.fix: Whatever action is to be done by this one,

issues.span: the joyful result of play
issues.evidence: 'རྩེད་མོའི་བདེ་འབྲས' = the result that is happiness/pleasure of play (Skt krīḍāphalasukha; bo-shenga 'རྩེད་མོའི་བདེ་བའི་འབྲས་བུ'); བདེ(་བ) is locked as 'happiness', and 'joyful' attaches to the result rather than naming what the result is.
issues.fix: the happiness that is the result of play

7-64.translation:
Like honey smeared on a razor's edge,
If one is not satiated by sensual desires,
With its ripening of happiness and peace,
How could one ever be satiated by merit?

issues.span:
With its ripening of happiness and peace,
How could one ever be satiated by merit?
issues.evidence: 'རྣམ་སྨིན་བདེ་ལ་ཞི་བ་ཡི། བསོད་ནམས་ཀྱིས་ལྟ་ཅི་སྟེ་ངོམས།' - 'རྣམ་སྨིན་བདེ་ལ་ཞི་བ་ཡི' modifies merit (bo-gyaltsab 7-64: merit gives happiness as ripening and leads to the peace of cessation). In the English 'With its ripening...' is a dangling modifier with no antecedent, and 'Like honey...' is likewise detached from 'sensual desires', which it qualifies ('འདོད་པ་རྣམས་ཀྱིས' ... 'སྤུ་གྲིའི་སོར་ཆགས་སྦྲང་རྩི་ལྟའི').
issues.fix: By merit, whose ripening is happiness and which is peaceful, how could one ever be satiated?

7-73.translation:
Thinking, "How, in these situations,
Will mindfulness become a habit?"
For this reason, one should seek encounters
Or appropriate actions.

issues.span: one should seek encounters
issues.evidence: ཕྲད་པ is left without an object in the root, but bo-kunpal 7-73 (བླ་མ་དགེ་བའི་བཤེས་གཉེན་དང་ཕྲད་པ), bo-shenga 7-73 (མཁན་པོ་དང་སློབ་དཔོན་... དང་ཕྲད་པ) and bo-gyaltsab 7-73 (ཐེག་པ་ཆེན་པོའི་དགེ་བའི་བཤེས་གཉེན་དང་འཕྲད་པ) all read it as meeting teachers or spiritual friends; Sanskrit saṃsarga is 'association'. Bare 'encounters' could be read as chance meetings of any kind.
issues.fix: one should seek out meeting (with teachers and spiritual friends)

8-9.translation:
If one shares the same fortune as a childish one,
One will certainly go to the lower realm;
If they lead one to unequal fortune,
What is the use of relying on a childish one?

issues.span: If they lead one to unequal fortune
issues.evidence: སྐལ་མི་མཉམ་པར་ཁྲིད་བྱེད་ན: bo-shenga 8-9 (འཕགས་པ་རྣམས་དང་སྐལ་བ་མི་མཉམ་པར་ཁྲིད་པར་བྱེད་ན), bo-gyaltsab 8-9 and bo-kunpal 8-9 say the fortune is unequal to that of the noble ones, i.e. they lead one away from the noble ones' destiny. The bare 'unequal fortune' leaves the comparandum open and, following the previous line, reads as unequal to the childish ones' fortune.
issues.fix: If they lead one to a fortune unlike that of the noble ones

8-30.translation:
Even this very body of mine,
By whose stench even foxes
Will not come near,
Will become exactly like that.

issues.span: Will become exactly like that.
issues.evidence: Tibetan དེ་ལྟ་བུར་ནི་འགྱུར་བར་འོང་ ('will come to become such'); the relative clause གང་གི་དྲི་ཡིས་... (by whose stench even jackals will not approach) qualifies the state the body will reach (bo-kunpal 8-30: ལུས་གང་གི་དྲིང་བ་... ཝ་... དྲུང་དུ་ཉེར་འགྲོ་མི་འགྱུར་བ་). The English leaves 'like that' without a clear antecedent, and 'exactly' has no counterpart in the Tibetan.
issues.fix: Will come to be such that, by its stench, even foxes will not come near.

8-35.translation:
Having made no friends and no enemies,
This body dwells alone in solitude;
Having reckoned it as already dead,
Even when dying, no one feels grief.

issues.span: Having reckoned it as already dead,
issues.evidence: The agent of the reckoning is others, not the body: bo-shenga 8-35 "ཉེ་དུ་སོགས་ཀྱིས་སྔ་ནས་ཤི་བ་དང་འདྲ་བར་བརྩིས་ན། ཤི་ནའང་དེའི་ཚེ་མྱ་ངན་བྱེད་པ་འགའ་ཡང་མེད་དོ"; bo-kunpal 8-35 "ཉེ་དུ་སོགས་ཀྱིས་སྔ་ནས་ཤི་བ་དང་འདྲར་བརྩིས་ནས". The English participle with "it" leaves the reckoner unclear.
issues.fix: Being reckoned by relatives and others as already dead,

8-38.translation:
Having let go of all other thoughts,
With a mind focused only on myself,
In order to settle the mind in meditative equipoise
And to subdue it, I shall strive.

issues.span: With a mind focused only on myself,
issues.evidence: "བདག་ལ་སེམས་པ་གཅིག་པུ་ཡིས" is explained as thinking solely of taming one's own mind / one's own practice: bo-shenga 8-38 "བདག་གི་སེམས་དུལ་བའི་ཐབས་ལ་སེམས་པ་གཅིག་པུ་ཡིས"; bo-kunpal 8-38 "བདག་གིས་རང་གི་སེམས་ལ་བལྟས་ཏེ"; Skt svacittaikāgramānasaḥ. "focused only on myself" can be read as self-concern.
issues.fix: With a mind intent solely on my own mind,

8-44.translation:
That face of your affliction,
just as it has now become manifest,
seeing it unveiled by vultures,
why do you flee from it now?

issues.span: That face of your affliction,
issues.evidence: bo-shenga 8-44 "ཁྱོད་ཉོན་མོངས་པར་གྱུར་པའི་གདོང་དེ" and bo-gyaltsab 8-44 "ཁྱོད་ཉོན་མོངས་ཤིང་ཆགས་པའི་གདོང་དེ" show the face is the one that afflicted you / that you were afflicted by and attached to; Skt tvatparikleśam. "face of your affliction" does not make this relation clear.
issues.fix: That face which afflicted you (the face you were afflicted by),

8-51.translation:
If you have no attachment to impurity,
To a cage of bones bound by sinews,
Plastered with the mud of flesh,
Why do you embrace another in your lap?

issues.span: To a cage of bones bound by sinews, / Plastered with the mud of flesh, / Why do you embrace another in your lap?
issues.evidence: The Tibetan "རུས་གཟེབ་རྒྱུས་པས་སྦྲེལ་བ་ལ། ཤ་ཡི་འདམ་གྱིས་ཞལ་ཞལ་བྱས། གཞན" qualifies "གཞན" (another); bo-shenga 8-51 glosses it as "གཞན་བུད་མེད་ཀྱི་ལུས་" (the other woman's body). The English "To a cage of bones" reads as a dangling indirect object, so the syntax of the object is unclear.
issues.fix: why do you embrace in your lap another—a cage of bones bound by sinews, plastered with the mud of flesh?

8-67.translation:
If, with long hair and nails,
Yellowish teeth, and imbued with the foul smell of mud,
The nature of the body
Is terrifying indeed when naked,

issues.span: Yellowish teeth
issues.evidence: Tibetan "སོ་སྐྱ་དྲིར་བཅས" = yellowish teeth together with filth/foulness (བཅས). bo-kunpal 8-67: "སོ་སྐྱ་བོ་ ... དྲི་མར་བཅས་པ" and bo-shenga 8-67: "སོ་སྐྱ་བོ་དྲི་མར་བཅས་པ" (teeth with filth); Sanskrit "dantaiḥ samalapāṇḍuraiḥ". The English drops the filth on the teeth.
issues.fix: yellowish teeth with filth

8-68.translation:
Like a weapon that harms oneself,
Why do you make efforts to polish it?
Through the efforts of those deluded regarding the self,
This earth is completely agitated by madmen.

issues.span: to polish it
issues.evidence: "བྱི་དོར་བྱེད" means to tidy, clean and tend. bo-kunpal 8-68 glosses it as "ཁྲུས་དང་བྱུག་པ་སོགས་ཀྱིས་བྱི་དོར་བྱེད" (washing, anointing and so on) of the body. "Polish" fits a weapon but not the body, which is what "it" refers to.
issues.fix: to tend to it (wash, anoint and adorn it)

8-79.translation:
For lustful persons, these and so forth
Are the many disadvantages, and the benefit is small,
Just as beasts that pull a cart
Eat only a few mouthfuls of grass.

issues.span: the benefit is small
issues.evidence: མནོག་ཆུང་ (Sanskrit alpāsvāda, 'little taste/relish'); bo-kunpal 8-79 glosses it as བདེ་བའི་མནོག་ཆུང་བ, a small taste of pleasure. མནོག is the savour of enjoyment, not 'benefit' (phan).
issues.fix: and the enjoyment (gratification) is slight

8-80.translation:
For the sake of that small benefit,
Which is not rare even for beasts to accomplish,
This perfect leisure and endowment, so difficult to find,
Is destroyed by those tormented by karma.

issues.span: that small benefit
issues.evidence: མནོག་ཆུང་ (Sanskrit āsvādalava) is a slight taste/relish of enjoyment; bo-kunpal 8-80 glosses it as མནོག་ཆུང་ལ་ ... ལོངས་སྤྱོད (food, clothing and other enjoyments). 'Benefit' misses this and is inconsistent with a proper rendering of མནོག.
issues.fix: that slight enjoyment

8-84.translation:
Having thus become weary of desire,
One should generate joy for solitude,
Empty of disputes and afflictions,
Within peaceful forests.

issues.span:
One should generate joy for solitude,
Empty of disputes and afflictions,
Within peaceful forests.
issues.evidence: རྩོད་དང་ཉོན་མོངས་ཀྱིས་སྟོང་པ། ཞི་བའི་ནགས་ཀྱི་ནང་དག་ཏུ། - 'empty of disputes and afflictions' qualifies the forests (bo-shenga 8-84: རྩོད་པ་དང་ནང་གི་ཉོན་མོངས་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་སྟོང་པ། ... ཞི་བའི་ནགས), but in the English the modifier follows 'solitude' and reads as describing solitude.
issues.fix:
One should generate joy for solitude
Within peaceful forests
Empty of disputes and afflictions.

8-87.translation:
Acting independently and without attachment,
Unconnected to anyone at all,
Whatever joy of contentment one enjoys,
That is difficult even for Indra to find.

issues.span: joy of contentment
issues.evidence: ཆོག་ཤེས་བདེ་སྤྱོད་ - བདེ་ is 'happiness' (bo-kunpal 8-87: ཆོག་ཤེས་པའི་བདེ་བ; bo-gyaltsab: ཆོག་ཤེས་པའི་བདེ་བ), rendered 'happiness' elsewhere in this passage; 'joy' suggests དགའ་བ.
issues.fix: happiness of contentment

issues.span: If not, I too am like sentient beings.
issues.evidence: Tibetan དེ་མིན་བདག་ཀྱང་སེམས་ཅན་བཞིན། is explained in bo-kunpal 8-102 and bo-shenga 8-102 as: if others' suffering is not to be averted, then my own suffering too, like that of other sentient beings, is not to be averted. The English leaves the point of comparison (non-aversion of suffering) unstated and reads as an unclear statement about the speaker's identity.
issues.fix: If not, then I too am like other sentient beings (my own suffering is not to be averted either).

8-109.translation:
Therefore, just as I protect myself
From even the slightest unpleasantness,
Likewise, a protective mind toward others
And a mind of compassion should be cultivated in this way.

issues.span: the slightest unpleasantness
issues.evidence: Tibetan མི་སྙན་ (Skt. avarṇa) is glossed in bo-kunpal 8-109 as མི་སྙན་པའི་ཚིག་ཙམ and in bo-shenga 8-109 as མི་སྙན་པ་བརྗོད་པ, i.e. an unpleasant or disparaging word, not unpleasantness in general.
issues.fix: even the slightest unpleasant word

8-112.translation:
Having known oneself to have faults and others too
To be an ocean of good qualities,
One should meditate on completely discarding self-grasping
And taking up others.

issues.span:
Having known oneself to have faults and others too
To be an ocean of good qualities
issues.evidence: བདག་ཉིད་སྐྱོན་བཅས་གཞན་ལ་ཡང་། ཡོན་ཏན་རྒྱ་མཚོར་ཤེས་བྱས་ནས། — "too" (ཡང་) goes with others as an ocean of good qualities (Sanskrit parān api guṇodadhīn; bo-kunpal 8-112 gives self = faults, others = qualities); the English can be read as "oneself and others too have faults".
issues.fix: Having known that oneself has faults, and that others too are oceans of good qualities,

8-114.translation:
Just as toward this body of selflessness,
Through habituation, the intellect of self has arisen,
Likewise, toward other sentient beings as well,
Through habituation, why would the intellect of self not arise?

issues.span: this body of selflessness
issues.evidence: བདག་མེད་ལུས་འདི་ལ། — བདག་མེད་ modifies ལུས་ ("this body that is selfless/without self"; Sanskrit svakāye 'smin nirātmake; bo-shenga 8-114 བདག་མེད་པའི་ལུས་). "Body of selflessness" implies the body belongs to selflessness.
issues.fix: this body, which is selfless (lacks a self)

8-117.translation:
Therefore, the Protector Avalokiteśvara,
Out of great compassion,
In order to dispel wandering beings' fear in assemblies,
Bestowed a blessing upon even his own name.

issues.evidence: འཁོར་གྱི་འཇིགས་པའང་བསལ་བའི་ཕྱིར། — the suffix འང "even" (Sanskrit pariṣacchāradyabhayam api) marks even the minor fear of timidity in assemblies (bo-kunpal 8-117 "བག་ཚ་བ་ཙམ་གྱི་འཇིགས་པའང་"); the English places "even" only on the name.
issues.fix: In order to dispel even wandering beings' fear in assemblies,

8-120.translation:
Through attachment to this body of mine,
Fear arises toward small sources of fear;
Toward that body which gives rise to fear,
Who would not be hostile as toward an enemy?

issues.span: be hostile as toward an enemy
issues.evidence: སྡང་མི་བྱེད། — སྡང་བ is "to hate/loathe" (Sanskrit na dviṣet; bo-kunpal 8-120 སྡང་བར་མི་བྱེད།), not "be hostile".
issues.fix: hate as an enemy

8-122.translation:
Whoever, for the sake of profit and respect,
Kills even their father and mother,
And, having stolen the wealth of the Three Jewels,
Will thereby be burned in the Avīci hell;

issues.span: Will thereby be burned in the Avīci hell;
issues.evidence: དེས་ནི་མནར་མེད་བསྲེག་འགྱུར་ན། — the clause ends in the conditional ན ("if"; bo-kunpal 8-122 ends "འགྱུར་ན"), continuing into 8-123's question. The English states it as an independent assertion.
issues.fix: If one is thereby burned in the Avīci hell,

8-124.translation:
"If I give, what will I consume?"
Thinking of one's own welfare is the way of a demon.
"If I consume, what will I give?"
Thinking of the welfare of others is the dharma of a god.

issues.span: the dharma of a god
issues.evidence: ལྷ་ཡི་ཆོས། — ཆོས here is "nature/way" parallel to འདྲེ་ཡི་ཚུལ (Sanskrit devarājatā "godliness"; bo-kunpal 8-124 ཆོས་ལུགས་བཟང་པོ, bo-shenga ལྷ་ཡི་རྒྱུར་གྱུར་པའི་ཆོས). "Dharma" suggests the Buddhist teaching.
issues.fix: the way of a god

8-141.translation:
I do all the work, and
this one remains in happiness itself.
This one is great in the world, and
I am known as inferior and without good qualities.

issues.span: all the work
issues.evidence: Tibetan ལས་རྣམས་བྱེད་པ་ is 'performing tasks/labors' (plural); no word for 'all'. bo-shenga 8-141 glosses these as menial labor (ཁུར་ཁྱེར་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་དམན་པའི་ལས་རྣམས་).
issues.fix: I perform the labors, and

8-146.translation:
Looking at one equal to me,
in order to make myself superior,
my gain and honor
will certainly be secured even through dispute.

issues.span: will certainly be secured
issues.evidence: Tibetan ངེས་པར་བསྒྲུབ is a resolve/obligation, not a prediction: bo-kunpal 8-146 'ངེས་པར་བསྒྲུབ་པར་བྱའོ', bo-gyaltsab 8-146 'ངེས་པར་བསྒྲུབ་པར་བྱའོ' (must be accomplished). Parallel verse 8-147 is rendered with 'I shall ensure'.
issues.fix: I shall certainly secure, even through dispute,

8-156.translation:
If, in former times,
You had performed this action,
A situation like this, other than the perfect happiness
Of a Buddha, could not possibly occur.

issues.span: A situation like this, other than the perfect happiness of a Buddha, could not possibly occur.
issues.evidence: Tibetan 'སངས་རྒྱས་ཕུན་སུམ་བདེ་མིན་པ། གནས་སྐབས་འདི་འདྲར་འགྱུར་མི་སྲིད།': 'མིན་པ' qualifies 'གནས་སྐབས་འདི་འདྲ' (a situation like this that is not Buddha's perfect happiness). bo-gyaltsab 8-156: 'སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་དོན་གཉིས་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པའི་བདེ་བ་མིན་པ་སྡུག་བསྔལ་མྱོང་བའི་གནས་སྐབས་འདི་འདྲ'. The English 'other than' reads as an exception clause and obscures that the current suffering is what is not Buddha's happiness.
issues.fix: such a situation as this, which is not the perfect happiness of a Buddha, could not possibly occur.

8-167.translation:
Yet, even when instructed in that way,
If you, my mind, do not act like that,
Since all faults rely upon you,
You yourself will simply be subdued.

issues.span: You yourself will simply be subdued.
issues.evidence: Tibetan 'ཁྱོད་ཉིད་ཚར་གཅད་བྱ་བར་ཟད།' is obligation/only-remaining-option ('བྱ་བ' gerundive), not a bare future passive; bo-shenga 8-167: 'ཁྱོད་ཉིད་ཚར་བཅད་པར་བྱ་བ་ཁོ་ནར་ཟད་དོ'; bo-kunpal: 'ཚར་བཅད་པར་བྱ་བར་ཟད་དོ' (to be subdued by the antidote). Skt 'tvām eva nigrahīṣyāmi' has the speaker as agent.
issues.fix: there is nothing left but to subdue you yourself.

9-4.translation:
Even yogis, due to differences in intellect,
Are invalidated by those successively higher,
Through examples accepted by both,
Because they are unanalyzed for the sake of the result.

issues.span: Because they are unanalyzed for the sake of the result.
issues.evidence: འབྲས་བུའི་དོན་དུ་མ་དཔྱད་ཕྱིར: bo-shenga 9-4 explains "འབྲས་བུའི་དོན་དུ་མ་དཔྱད་པར་དེའི་རྒྱུ་ལ་འཇུག་པའི་ཕྱིར" (one engages in the causes without analyzing, for the sake of the result); bo-kunpal "འབྲས་བུའི་དོན་དུ་མ་བརྟགས་མ་དཔྱད་པར". The English leaves the subject of 'unanalyzed' unclear and reads as if the result is unanalyzed.
issues.fix: Because, for the sake of the result, they are not analyzed.

9-6.translation:
Even the direct perception of forms and so forth
Is through convention, not through valid cognition.
Regarding impurity and so forth,
That is false, like the convention of purity and so forth.

issues.span:
Regarding impurity and so forth,
That is false, like the convention of purity and so forth.
issues.evidence: Tibetan: དེ་ནི་མི་གཙང་ལ་སོགས་ལ། གཙང་སོགས་གྲགས་པ་བཞིན་དུ་རྫུན། The phrase 'regarding impurity' (མི་གཙང་ལ་སོགས་ལ) belongs with the convention of purity (གཙང་སོགས་གྲགས་པ), as bo-kunpal 9-6 shows (the body of a woman is impure, yet is conventionally called pure). The English attaches it to 'That is false', so 'purity regarding impurity' is lost.
issues.fix:
That is false, just as the convention of purity and so forth
regarding impure things and so forth is false.

9-9.translation:
Merit from a Victor like an illusion
Is just as it is for one who is truly existent.
"If sentient beings are like illusions,
How are they born after dying?"

issues.span:
Merit from a Victor like an illusion
Is just as it is for one who is truly existent.
issues.evidence: Tibetan ཇི་ལྟར ('how?') in line 2 is the opponent's question, and ཇི་བཞིན ('just as') is the reply. bo-gyaltsab 9-9 and bo-kunpal 9-9 read the pair as objection plus answer. The English drops 'how' and gives only a flat statement, with no marking that the first part is the objection and the second part the reply.
issues.fix:
"How is there merit from a Victor like an illusion?"
[Reply:] Just as it is for one who is truly existent.

9-26.translation:
If an illusion is not other than the mind,
And yet it is not conceived of as not other,
If it is an entity, how is it not other?
If it is not other, it does not exist as an entity.

issues.span: And yet it is not conceived of as not other
issues.evidence: Tibetan གཞན་མིན་པར་ཡང་མི་རྟག་ = "nor is it posited as non-other (identical)"; bo-kunpal 9-26 glosses སེམས་དང་གཅིག་ཡིན་པར་ཡང་མི་བརྟགས (not posited as one with the mind). "And yet ... not other" adds an adversative and the double negative hides that the claim is neither different nor identical.
issues.fix: And it is not conceived as non-other (identical) either,

9-27.translation:
Just as an illusion, although not true,
Is what is seen, so too is the perceiving mind.
"If saṃsāra is based on an entity,
Otherwise it would be like space."

issues.span: Is what is seen, so too is the perceiving mind.
issues.evidence: Tibetan བལྟ་བྱ་དེ་བཞིན་ལྟ་བྱེད་ཡིད། and bo-kunpal 9-27 (ལྟ་བྱེད་ཡིད་ཀྱང་སྒྱུ་མ་ལྟ་བུའི་བདེན་མེད་ཡིན་ཀྱང་ལྟ་བྱེད་དུ་འཐད): the mind is the perceiver though untrue; English "so too is the perceiving mind" could be read as the mind also being seen.
issues.fix: Is something to be seen, so too the mind is the one who sees.

9-29.translation:
When the mind is free of an apprehended object,
At that time, all are Tathāgatas.
Even if that is so, what merit is there
In conceptually constructing Cittamātra?

issues.span: what merit is there
issues.evidence: ཡོན་ཏན་ཅི་ཞིག་ཡོད: bo-kunpal 9-29 and bo-gyaltsab 9-29 gloss ཡོན་ཏན་ as དགོས་པ (purpose/benefit); Sanskrit guṇa. "Merit" suggests puṇya (བསོད་ནམས).
issues.fix: what benefit is there

9-30.translation:
Even if one knows things to be like an illusion,
How will the afflictions be averted?
Since, toward an illusory woman,
Even her creator generates attachment.

issues.span: entire verse (unquoted)
issues.evidence: bo-gyaltsab 9-30 and bo-shenga 9-30 (…ཞེ་ན།) show the whole verse is the opponent's objection; other objections in this chapter are quoted, but here it reads as the author's own assertion.
issues.fix: Put the verse in quotation marks as the objector's speech.

9-31.translation:
Her creator, toward objects of knowledge,
Has not abandoned the latent tendencies of the afflictions.
Therefore, when he sees her,
His latent tendency for emptiness is weak.

issues.span: His latent tendency for emptiness is weak.
issues.evidence: སྟོང་ཉིད་བག་ཆགས is locked as "latent tendency of emptiness" (used in 9-32); bo-gyaltsab 9-31 glosses སྟོང་ཉིད་རྟོགས་པའི་བག་ཆགས. "for" departs from the locked phrase.
issues.fix: His latent tendency of emptiness is weak.

9-37.translation:
In accordance with the conduct of awakening,
The shrine of the Victor has been accomplished;
Even when the bodhisattva has passed
Into nirvāṇa, it accomplishes all aims.

issues.evidence: Tibetan རྒྱལ་བའི་མཆོད་སྡོང་བསྒྲུབས་པ་ཡང་ and Sanskrit jinastambho 'pi: the particle ཡང (also/even) is not rendered; bo-kunpal 9-37 and bo-gyaltsab 9-37 link it to the garuḍa simile ("likewise").
issues.fix: Likewise, the shrine of the Victor, too, is accomplished in accordance with the conduct of awakening;

9-42.translation:
By whatever conditions you believe in that,
That is the same for the Mahāyāna as well.
If it is true because two others accept it,
The Vedas and so forth would also be true.

issues.span: because two others accept it
issues.evidence: Tibetan གཞན་གཉིས་འདོད་པས; bo-shenga 9-42: གཞན་གང་ཡང་རུང་བ་གཉིས (any two others), bo-kunpal 9-42 similarly གཞན་གང་ཟག་གང་ཡང་རུང་བ་གཉིས. "two others" does not make clear it means any two parties.
issues.fix: because any two other parties accept it

9-44.translation:
If being a monk is the root of the teaching,
Even being a monk is difficult to maintain.
For those whose minds have apprehension,
Even nirvāṇa is difficult to maintain.

issues.span: difficult to maintain
issues.evidence: Tibetan དཀའ་བར་གནས; bo-kunpal 9-44 glosses ཡོད་པར་དཀའ and ཐོབ་པར་དཀའ་བར་གནས (hard to exist / hard to attain); bo-gyaltsab 9-44: ཐོབ་པར་ཐལ (would not be attained). "Maintain" implies upkeep of an existing state, whereas the point is that such a monk/nirvāṇa is hard to realize or establish.
issues.fix: is difficult to establish (hard to come by)

9-46.translation:
If you say it is certain that, for the time being,
The craving for grasping does not exist,
Even if that craving is not afflicted,
Why would it not exist, just like delusion?

issues.span: The craving for grasping
issues.evidence: ཉེར་ལེན་སྲེད་པ: bo-kunpal 9-46 glosses ཉེར་ལེན་ as ཉེ་བར་ལེན་པའི་རྒྱུ་སྲེད་པ, i.e. craving that is the cause of grasping (Skt tṛṣṇā ... upādānam); grasping is not the object of the craving.
issues.fix: the craving that is the cause of grasping

9-49.translation:
If any speech that accords with the sūtras
Is asserted to be spoken by the Buddha,
Is it not asserted that most of the Mahāyāna
Is equal to your sūtras?

issues.span: accords with the sūtras
issues.evidence: ངག་གང་མདོ་སྡེ་ལ་འཇུག: འཇུག means enters/is included in (Skt sūtre ’vatared); bo-kunpal 9-49 and bo-shenga 9-49 read it as speech that enters/appears in the sūtra collection, not merely accords with it.
issues.fix: enters the sūtras

9-52.translation:
For the sake of those suffering through delusion,
Being freed from the extremes of attachment and fear
To successfully remain in saṃsāra—
This is the result of emptiness.

issues.span: To successfully remain in saṃsāra
issues.evidence: འཁོར་བར་གནས་པ་གྲུབ་འགྱུར་བ: remaining in saṃsāra is what comes to be accomplished (Skt saṃsāre sidhyati sthitiḥ); the infinitive reads as a purpose of being freed, which the Tibetan does not state (bo-kunpal 9-52: ... འཁོར་བར་གནས་པར་འགྲུབ་པར་འགྱུར་བ).
issues.fix: Remaining in saṃsāra is accomplished

9-53.translation:
Thus, toward the position of emptiness,
Refutation is not appropriate.
Therefore, without any doubt,
One should meditate on emptiness.

issues.span: not appropriate
issues.evidence: འཐད་མ་ཡིན: འཐད་པ means tenable/valid (Skt nopapadyate); bo-gyaltsab 9-53 says refutation is untenable because it is harmed by reasoning, not that it is improper.
issues.fix: is not tenable

9-64.translation:
Thus, sattva, rajas, and
Tamas are neither a son nor a father,
And it is not seen to have a nature
That possesses the apprehension of sound.

issues.span: it is not seen to have a nature
issues.evidence: དེ་ནི་སྒྲ་འཛིན་དང་ལྡན་པའི་རང་བཞིན་དུ་ནི་མཐོང་མ་ཡིན: bo-shenga 9-64 identifies the subject as གཟུགས་འཛིན་པ་པོ་དེ, the apprehender of form; English "it" has no clear referent after the plural sattva, rajas, tamas.
issues.fix: that apprehender of form is not seen to have a nature

9-91.translation:
If, because an opposing condition has arisen,
Suffering does not arise,
Is it not established that the conception of feeling
Is merely conceptual clinging?

issues.span:
the conception of feeling
Is merely conceptual clinging
issues.evidence: ཚོར་བར་རྟོག་པ་མངོན་ཞེན་ཉིད། ཡིན་ཞེས་བྱ་བར་གྲུབ་མིན་ནམ། Sanskrit 'kalpanābhiniveśo hi vedanā' says feeling itself is conceptual clinging; bo-kunpal 9-91: ཚོར་བ་ཞེས་བྱ་བར་ནང་གི་རྟོག་པ་ཡིས་... མངོན་པར་ཞེན་པ་... ཉིད་ཡིན་ — what is called 'feeling' is nothing but clinging due to conception. The English makes the 'conception of feeling' the thing identified with clinging.
issues.fix:
that what is called feeling
is nothing but conceptual clinging

9-99.translation:
Seeing or even touching
Is of a nature like a dream and an illusion;
Because it arises simultaneously with the mind,
Feeling is not seen by it.

issues.span:
Because it arises simultaneously with the mind,
Feeling is not seen by it.
issues.evidence: སེམས་དང་ལྷན་ཅིག་སྐྱེས་པའི་ཕྱིར། ཚོར་བ་དེ་ཡིས་མཐོང་མ་ཡིན། The one arising together with the mind is the feeling, and 'that' (དེ་ཡིས, Skt tena) is the mind (bo-kunpal 9-99: ཚོར་བ་དེ་སེམས་དེ་ཡིས་མཐོང་བ་མ་ཡིན; bo-shenga 9-99). English 'it ... it' could be read as the seeing/touching in line 1.
issues.fix:
Because feeling arises simultaneously with the mind,
it is not seen by that mind.

9-101.translation:
There is no feeler at all,
Therefore feeling does not exist in reality.
Thus, for this collection of selflessness,
How could it be harmed by this?

issues.span: for this collection of selflessness
issues.evidence: བདག་མེད་ཚོགས་འདི་ལ། — 'this collection that lacks a self' (bo-shenga 9-101: བདག་མེད་པ་རྟེན་ཅིང་འབྲེལ་བར་འབྱུང་བའི་ཚོགས་པ་འདི་ལ; bo-kunpal: བདག་མེད་པར་ཕུང་པོའི་ཚོགས་པ). Sanskrit 'nirātmake kalāpe'. 'Collection of selflessness' treats selflessness as what is collected.
issues.fix: for this collection, which is selfless (without a self),

9-114.translation:
A sprout arises from a seed, and
Just as the seed is known by that very sprout,
By the consciousness arisen from the object of knowledge,
Why is its existence not known?

issues.span: A sprout arises from a seed, and / Just as the seed is known by that very sprout, / By the consciousness arisen from the object of knowledge, / Why is its existence not known?
issues.evidence: The verse is the opponent's objection: bo-kunpal 9-114 opens "ཡང་དེ་དག་འདི་སྙམ་དུ..." and ends "...ཅིས་མི་རྟོགས་ཏེ་རྟོགས་སོ་ཞེ་ན"; bo-shenga 9-114 ends "...ཅིས་མི་རྟོགས་ཞེ་ན། འདི་ནི་དཔེ་དང་འདྲ་བ་མ་ཡིན་ནོ" (the reply comes in 9-115). The translation leaves it unmarked, whereas the parallel objections 9-106 and 9-109 are set in quotation marks, so the reader cannot tell who speaks.
issues.fix: "A sprout arises from a seed, and / Just as the seed is known by that very sprout, / By the consciousness arisen from the object of knowledge, / Why is its existence not known?" (set in quotation marks as the opponent's objection)

9-151.translation:
Thus, regarding entities that are empty,
What is there to gain and what is there to lose?
By whom is respect shown,
Or what is there to be completely despised?

issues.span:
By whom is respect shown,
Or what is there to be completely despised?
issues.evidence: Tibetan གང་གིས་རིམ་གྲོ་བྱས་པའམ། ཡོངས་སུ་བརྙས་པའང་ཅི་ཞིག་ཡོད། has a single question 'what is there' governing both being honored by anyone and being despised (bo-shenga 9-151: སེམས་ཅན་གང་གིས་བསྟོད་ཅིང་རིམ་གྲོ་བྱས་པའམ། སྨད་དེ་ཡོངས་སུ་བརྙས་པར་བྱས་པའང་ཅི་ཞིག་ཡོད). The English splits it into 'by whom is respect shown' and 'what is there to be despised', so the two parallel members no longer match and the agent 'by whom' attaches only to respect.
issues.fix: What is there in being honored or utterly despised by anyone?

9-158.translation:
Furthermore, the incomparable, unbearable
Ocean of suffering is boundless.
There, one thus has little strength,
And there, the lifespan is also short.

issues.span: Furthermore,
issues.evidence: Tibetan དེ་ཡང་ (Sanskrit tatra ca; bo-kunpal 9-158 and bo-shenga 9-158 read དེར་ཡང་ 'even there') refers back to existence (srid pa) of the previous verse; 'Furthermore' drops the locative 'there'.
issues.fix: There too,

9-160.translation:
Life passes quickly and meaninglessly,
And analysis is extremely hard to find.
Furthermore, as for habituation to distraction,
Where is the means to reverse it?

issues.span: Furthermore,
