issues.evidence: Tibetan དེར་ཡང་ (Sanskrit tatrāpi; bo-kunpal 9-160 འཁོར་བའི་གནས་དེར་ཡང་) means 'even there, in that place'; the same words are rendered 'Even there' in 9-159 and 9-161, but here 'Furthermore' drops the locative and breaks the anaphora.
issues.fix: Even there, as for habituation to distraction,

9-166.translation:
Thus, for those tormented by the fire of suffering,
Well-arisen from the clouds of merit,
With a rain of my own accumulation of happiness,
When will I pacify them?

issues.span:
for those tormented by the fire of suffering,
Well-arisen from the clouds of merit,
issues.evidence: Tibetan བསོད་ནམས་སྤྲིན་ལས་ལེགས་འཁྲུངས་པའི། modifies རང་གི་བདེ་བའི་ཚོགས་ཆར ("rain of my own accumulation of happiness"), not the tormented beings; bo-kunpal 9-166: བསོད་ནམས་ཀྱི་ཚོགས་ཚད་མེད་པའི་སྤྲིན་ལས་ལེགས་པར་བྱུང་བའི་རང་གི་བདེ་བའི་ཚོགས་ཆར; bo-shenga 9-166 likewise. In the English, the dangling line can be read as describing the beings.
issues.fix: Well-arisen from the clouds of merit—a rain of my own accumulation of happiness—

10-1.translation:
By my having composed
Engaging in the Conduct of Awakening,
Through whatever virtue that is, may all wandering beings
Engage in the conduct of awakening.

issues.span:
By my having composed
Engaging in the Conduct of Awakening,
Through whatever virtue that is
issues.evidence: Tibetan has a single relation: བདག་གིས...བརྩམས་པ་ཡི། དགེ་བ་གང་དེས "by whatever virtue [arises] from my composing (the treatise) Engaging in the Conduct of Awakening"; bo-shenga 10-1: བསྟན་བཅོས་རྣམ་པར་བརྩམས་པ་ཡི། དགེ་བ་གང་ཡིན་པ་དེས. The English gives two stacked instrumentals ("By my having composed... Through whatever virtue that is"), which reads as garbled.
issues.fix:
Through whatever virtue there is in my having composed
Engaging in the Conduct of Awakening,

10-12.translation:
By the falling of a rain of flowers mixed with scented water,
Seeing the burning embers of hell extinguished with a hiss,
And thinking, "What is this sudden satisfaction with bliss?"
May the hell beings behold Padmapāṇi.

issues.span: burning embers of hell
issues.evidence: Tibetan དམྱལ་བའི་མེ་མདག "the fire and embers of hell"; bo-shenga 10-12: དམྱལ་བའི་མེ་དང་མདག་མ་དག; bo-kunpal 10-12: དམྱལ་བའི་མེ་མདག. English drops "fire" as a separate item.
issues.fix: fires and embers of hell

10-15.translation:
Likewise, by my roots of virtue, upon seeing Samantabhadra and other
Bodhisattvas' unobstructed clouds, and the bliss
And cool, fragrant rain they let fall,
May those sentient beings of hell become manifestly joyful.

issues.span:
and the bliss
And cool, fragrant rain they let fall
issues.evidence: Tibetan བདེ་བ་དང་། བསིལ་ཞིང་དྲི་ཞིམ་དང་ལྡན་ཆར་པ: "bliss" is one of the qualities of the rain (blissful, cool, fragrant), not a separate thing let fall; bo-shenga 10-15: རེག་ན་བདེ་བ་དང་། བསིལ་ཞིང་དྲི་ཞིམ་པོའི་ངད་པ་དང་ལྡན་པའི་ཆར་པ; bo-gyaltsab 10-15: བདེ་བ་དང་བསིལ་ཞིང་དྲི་ཞིམ་པ་དང་ལྡན་པའི་ཆར་བ. "the bliss and cool, fragrant rain" can be read as two nouns.
issues.fix:
and the blissful,
cool, fragrant rain they let fall

issues.span: those afflicted by sorrow
issues.evidence: Tibetan མྱ་ངན་ཉམ་ཐག་ has two terms, sorrow and ཉམ་ཐག་ (distressed, wretched); bo-kunpal 10-20 glosses མྱ་ངན་གྱིས་གདུངས་ཤིང་ཉམ་ཐག་པ་རྣམས་, bo-shenga མྱ་ངན་གྱིས་ཉམ་ཐག་པ་; the English renders only 'sorrow'.
issues.fix: those who are wretched with sorrow

10-26.translation:
In fearful, pathless wildernesses and the like,
Children, the elderly, the unprotected,
And those asleep, intoxicated, or insane—
May the gods protect them.

issues.span: intoxicated, or insane
issues.evidence: Tibetan མྱོས་ཤིང་རབ་མྱོས་རྣམས་ is 'intoxicated and utterly intoxicated'; bo-kunpal 10-26 རབ་ཏུ་མྱོས་པས་བག་མེད་པར་གྱུར་ཏེ (very drunk, hence heedless), bo-shenga མྱོས་ཤིང་རབ་ཏུ་མྱོས་པ; Sanskrit pramatta (heedless). Nothing says insane.
issues.fix: intoxicated, or utterly intoxicated

10-38.translation:
May they always meet with the Buddhas
And the children of the Buddhas.
With boundless clouds of offerings,
May they make offerings to the teachers of wandering beings.

issues.span: the teachers of wandering beings
issues.evidence: Tibetan 'འགྲོ་བའི་བླ་མ་མཆོད་པར་ཤོག' has no plural marker, Sanskrit 'jagadguru' is singular, and bo-gyaltsab 10-38 glosses it as the single 'འགྲོ་བའི་བླ་མ་སངས་རྒྱས'; the locked term 'teacher of wandering beings' is singular (the plural 'རྣམས' occurs only in the commentary's 'with retinue' gloss).
issues.fix: the teacher of wandering beings

10-42.translation:
May monasteries, with reading
And adorned with recitation, be well established.
May the Saṅgha always be in harmony,
And may the purposes of the Saṅgha be accomplished.

issues.span:
May monasteries, with reading
And adorned with recitation, be well established.
issues.evidence: Tibetan 'ཀློག་པ་དང་། ཁ་ཐོན་གྱིས་བརྒྱན་' pairs reading and recitation as joint adornments of the monasteries (Sanskrit 'pāṭhasvādhyāyakalilāḥ'; bo-gyaltsab 10-42 'ཀློག་པ་དང་ཁ་ཏོན་གྱིས་དར་ཞིང་རྒྱས་'). The English splits them awkwardly ('with reading' / 'adorned with recitation'), which is hard to parse.
issues.fix: May monasteries, adorned with reading and recitation, be well established.

10-45.translation:
Disillusioned by broken ethical discipline,
May they always exhaust their misdeeds.
Having also attained a happy realm,
May their ascetic discipline not decline even there.

issues.span:
Disillusioned by broken ethical discipline,
May they always exhaust their misdeeds.
issues.evidence: Tibetan 'ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་འཆལ་བས་ཡིད་བྱུང་ནས' refers to those whose discipline has become corrupt who turn weary of it (bo-shenga 10-45 'སྔར་བསླབ་པ་ཉམས་པ་དག་ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་འཆལ་བས་ཡིད་བྱུང་སྟེ'; Sanskrit 'duḥśīlāḥ santu saṃvignāḥ'). The English has no stated subject, so 'they' wrongly picks up the ordained of the previous stanza, and 'disillusioned by broken ethical discipline' could mean disenchanted with the breaking of it.
issues.fix: May those whose ethical discipline has been broken become weary of it, and always exhaust their misdeeds.

10-54.translation:
As far as the limits of space in the ten directions,
In order to accomplish the welfare of all sentient beings,
Just as Mañjuśrī acts,
May my conduct also be like that.

issues.span: As far as the limits of space in the ten directions,
issues.evidence: Tibetan 'ཕྱོགས་བཅུའི་ནམ་མཁའི་མཐས་གཏུགས་པའི། སེམས་ཅན་ཀུན' is an attributive phrase qualifying 'sentient beings' (Sanskrit 'daśadigvyomaparyanta-sarvasattvārtha'; bo-kunpal 10-54 'ནམ་མཁའི་མཐས་གཏུགས་པར་ཁྱབ་པའི་སེམས་ཅན་མ་ལུས་པ'). The English leaves the phrase as a dangling adverbial that can be read as modifying 'accomplish' or 'acts'.
issues.fix: In order to accomplish the welfare of all sentient beings, as far as the limits of space in the ten directions,
